    2027 NBA Draft Big Board: Quentin Coleman's meteoric rise, Tyran Stokes stays at No. 1, returners boost stock

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the first thing to know about the 2027 draft cycle is that it remains wide open.
    • But after three full weeks of college basketball and heading into a Thanksgiving week full of high-profile matchups, we have updated the 2027 NBA Draft Big Board.
    • Inside the front offices of the 30 NBA organizations, most have yet to even start ranking prospects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the first thing to know about the 2027 draft cycle is that it remains wide open. There are still eight months to go before Adam Silver steps up to the podium to announce the first pick. Nothing has been decided yet. In fact, there's probably only about ten players total that can confidently say they expect to be a first-round pick at this point. Everything else is yet to be determined.

    But after three full weeks of college basketball and heading into a Thanksgiving week full of high-profile matchups, we have updated the 2027 NBA Draft Big Board.

    Inside the front offices of the 30 NBA organizations, most have yet to even start ranking prospects. They're still building their lists, sorting them into tiers, and will spend the coming months trying to establish their order.

    According to recent reports, that's the biggest difference between those front offices and the public discourse about the draft. The fans want answers now, and the Twitter scouts are quick to make bold statements in hopes of saying they were right first. The experts who actually do this for a living recognize that the sole goal is to be right on draft night, and doing that requires them to not jump to any early conclusions.

    That's all critical context to understanding this massive board update, which is, at best, a way too early look at the most relevant prospects. It should be interpreted in tiers. There are probably five or six prospects competing for the top of the draft, but that list could change. Maybe 11 who should feel good about their chances to be first-round picks. Everything beyond that is simply a battle that will continue to play out over the course of the next 8 months. Let's dive into the biggest storylines after three weeks of college basketball action.

    Industry observers note that I got a first-hand look at Stokes last week at the Player's Era 8 in Las Vegas. He went down with a contusion midway through his first game, sat out the second, and returned to drop 22 points and 11 rebounds in the final. In totality, the signs of extreme growth that have characterized his early season play continued to be evident in Vegas. He was far and away the most talented player in high school basketball a year ago, but had developed a history of not living up to his potential, or at least not impacting winning to the degree that someone with his talent should. So, coming into his year at Kansas, the eyeballs were more about his maturity, reliability, and approach. Answering those questions has gone about as well as it possibly could so far. He's not only been engaged and impactful, but he's shown connectivity with Bill Self that makes him look coachable. He's also not gotten easily derailed by adversity, which is a reassuring data point.

    Industry observers note that to be clear, for as good as he's been, there's still plenty of room for improvement. In high school, he had an instinctive way of improvising his way to the rim. In college, he's found that isn't quite as easy, even with someone like Tre Kaufman-Renn regularly clearing the way for him anytime he comes charging at the rim. So, while he's over-dribbling at times, his playmaking is real, he's asserted himself as a rebounder, his shooting is progressing, and he's starting to use his size in the post.

    The bottom line is this: most teams are looking for a potential alpha-type creator with the first pick. Stokes is your best bet in the 2027 cycle, by a relatively large margin at this point, but it's still too early to say he's a lock to go number one. I'd put that at about 70% at this point. Getting to the finish line will require him to continue trending in the right direction, making sure teams are comfortable with their due diligence in the pre-draft process, and also leaving open the possibility for someone else to emerge in the coming months.

    In a recent development, speaking of ascending prospects, no one has moved the needle more in the first three weeks of the season than Illinois' freshman Quentin Coleman. But for those who track draft prospects 365 days a year, the last three weeks are just a short spurt in what has been a rapid rise over the course of the last 15 months.

    It has been revealed that in the 2025 EYBL season, Coleman averaged 11.8 points. 5.1 rebounds and 2.4 assists for a Brad Beal Elite team that won the Peach Jam Championship. To put it plainly, he was a role player, albeit a valuable one, on a team that was built around current Arkansas freshman JJ Andrews and utilized Trey Pearson, who is currently a freshman at High Point, as their primary ball-handler and distributor.

    As soon as Coleman's high school season began, though, we immediately saw signs of growth. Those signs continued throughout the course of the year, and he skyrocketed the rankings in the process. He also decommitted from Wake Forest and took a much bigger NIL payday from Illinois. While he finished with five-star status, it was immediately clear at the USA Basketball trials in May that even that was too low.

    Industry observers note that since arriving at Illinois, Coleman has continued the pattern of exceeding expectations. His skill level, feel for the game, defensive instincts, and nose for the ball are all as impressive as expected. The physical transition has been easier than expected. He's continued to develop more burst, physicality, and, as a result, playmaking.

    At the moment, he's moved all the way up to No. 4 on the CBS's current 2027 NBA Draft Big Board, but we're not going to put a cap on what he could do given the unprecedented growth we've witnessed over the last 15 months.

    In a recent development, there were a number of prospects who had a chance to be first-round picks in last year's draft, who opted to return to college basketball. While most, if not all, of them are probably making more money in college this year than they would have in the NBA, they are also making strides with their game, and in the process, helping their draft stock in what is widely viewed as a weaker draft than last year's.

    We've been bullish on Amari Allen's chances of helping himself given his new on-ball role at Alabama, and so far, he's done just that. The 16 points, 6 assists, and 5 rebounds per game on 52/50/82 shooting showcases both the versatility and shooting gains we were banking on. Most of all, though, it's his decision-making with the ball that has been glaring. His usage has gone way up, and his turnovers have gone way down. He has recorded 30 assists against just three turnovers through the first five games of the season. Add his hyper-competitiveness to the equation, and he's certainly helping himself.

    Sources indicate that arizona big man Motiejus Krivas looked like an NBA-ready defender last year. This year, it's been more of the same. He's massive, even by NBA standards, at 7-foot-2 and 260 pounds, but deceptively versatile and very smart with his angles. We're also seeing definite growth offensively, particularly with his skill set facing the basket. Last week's 18-point, 12-rebound, 4-block performance against UConn was one that captured all of his value, and a game that scouts will undoubtedly revisit.

    Meanwhile, his teammate, Ivan Kharchenkov, has gone from a defensive role player to Arizona's featured scorer, and is putting up nearly 23 points, 8 rebounds, and 5 assists per game. To put it plainly, he's been as good of a two-way player as there is in the country, and now looks like he could be trending towards the draft lottery.

    Florida's Thomas Haugh had a chance to be a mid-first-round pick last June, but the variable that gave many scouts pause was his shooting. This year, he's shooting it with much more confidence and rhythm, making 18 of his 34 attempts through his first five games. Simultaneously, he's continuing to do all the little things that made him so intriguing in the first place with his motor, physicality, rebounding, and defensive versatility.

    Industry observers note that speaking of shooting, Braylon Mullins is establishing himself as one of the nation's premier shooters, as expected, despite the fact that he's clearly not 100% healthy. Through his first five games, he's made 19 threes on 50 attempts, but it's been the types of shots that have really stood out. He's running all over the court, flying off screens, and making threes on the move, all while being the focal point of opposing defenses. In short, Mullins is making the type of tough shots that translate to the next level, despite not having his typical ability to separate.

    One of the defining characteristics of the national 2026 recruiting class was the number of prospects who had glaring potential, but had yet to put it all together. That list included the likes of Duke's Cameron Williams,  Ohio State's Anthony Thompson, Maryland's Baba Oladotun, Christian Collins,  Adonis Rayliff and Darius Ratliff, all at USC. Nevertheless, almost all of them commanded the type of recruitment and correlating financial commitment that suggested programs were willing to invest in their development.

    Sources indicate that so far In t those investments have not resulted in the types of gains we had hoped for. The Ratliffs, Adonis in particular, have indicated some flashes, while Collins has only recently been cleared. Williams and Oladotun are barely in the rotation, and Thompson is playing, but not making the type of impact that anyone hoped.

    It has been revealed that now, despite the lack of immediate return at the college level, most NBA decision-makers are still playing the long game, so I wouldn't expect any of these guys to be given up on just yet. Nevertheless, their early struggles did have to be accounted for on the massive board, which is why many of them are now outside the top 30.

    Latest Update: NBA trade rumors: Lakers planning to be active, Jazz looking elsewhere after Kyrie Irving buzz

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, we're now a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while we're still weeks away from the unofficial start of trade season (Dec.
    • It has been revealed that firm rumors are still in short supply, but we're at least getting some early buzz on who intends to do what in the months to come.
    • Recent findings suggest that the 14-3 Los Angeles Lakers are headed for a titanic clash with the San Antonio Spurs on Friday that will presumably put one of those two teams in pole position in the Western Conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, we're now a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while we're still weeks away from the unofficial start of trade season (Dec. 15), we've seen enough basketball for teams to at least begin making plans for the upcoming transaction cycle. Teams are starting to know how good they are, what sort of holes they're dealing with and what the market is going to look like as we draw closer to the February trade deadline.

    It has been revealed that firm rumors are still in short supply, but we're at least getting some early buzz on who intends to do what in the months to come. So let's check in on what has made the rounds lately.

    Recent findings suggest that the 14-3 Los Angeles Lakers are headed for a titanic clash with the San Antonio Spurs on Friday that will presumably put one of those two teams in pole position in the Western Conference. Last Friday, however, head of basketball operations Rob Pelinka did a pregame interview with Spectrum SportsNet in which he made it clear he looks to be aggressive ahead of February's deadline.

    Recent findings suggest that "We'll be active at the trade deadline to shore up things that we see," Pelinka stated. "We think this team has a real chance to make a run, so we want to give the group as much talent as we can. Don't want to get too far over our skis with a hot start, because you don't want to get substantial-headed, but clearly the way it's gone so far, it's been great and we hope it continues.".

    The Lakers are very limited in terms of tradable draft capital because of their big July swing for Walker Kessler. They only have one first-round asset available, and it's only swap rights in 2032. They picked up two useful second-round picks in the Deandre Ayton trade, though, giving them three in total. That's not enough for a blockbuster, but it's helpful liquidity. Further, the Lakers are relatively financially flexible going into the deadline as well. They're barely over the luxury-tax line and have around $8 million in room beneath their first apron hard cap, allowing them to potentially make a somewhat unbalanced trade if the need presents itself.

    So, what would the Lakers be looking for at the deadline? Two obvious needs stand out:.

    As Marc Stein noted, the Los Angeles Clippers have moved to a veteran-only starting lineup, with Darius Garland, Rui Hachimura, Derrick Jones Jr., Max Strus and Brook Lopez opening games lately. Brandon Ingram, returning Monday, is sure to join that group, and Kris Dunn is a central part of their rotation. All of these players but Ingram and Garland are on expiring deals, and Stein noted that the Clippers are "regarded as a certain seller" ahead of the trade deadline.

    It has been revealed that and, well, that makes plenty of sense. The Clippers were just stripped of five first-round picks in the Kawhi Leonard scandal. Those expiring contracts belong to players who almost certainly won't be a part of the next great Clipper team, but they could help replenish the team's draft capital moving forward.

    It has been revealed that the Clippers are, by far, the most versatile seller on the market right now. In theory, they could burnish just about any contender. Need defense? Jones and Dunn have you covered. Offense? Strus and Hachimura are proven playoff snipers. The center market is in the middle of a supply-demand crisis. Lopez has been sensational this season and could give any contender a solid 20 minutes per night. With Keaton Wagler in the building, it's hard to imagine they'd even shut the door on a good enough Garland offer. Expect the Clippers to live in the rumor mill for the next few months. They have several players who could legitimately impact the championship hunt.

    Last week, SNY dropped a stunner of a rumor: that the Utah Jazz, loaded with young guards and off to a terrible start, had had internal conversations about pursuing Mavericks guard Kyrie Irving. The rumor didn't make much sense in the moment, and The Salt Lake Tribune reported Monday that the Jazz "don't appear to have any real interest" in the future Hall of Famer.

    They have, however, talked trade with the team we just discussed: the Clippers. Those conversations began with "various Clippers bigs" and have moved on to wing depth, of which the Clippers have plenty. The Jazz are reportedly casting a wide net in pursuit of help.

    The 3-15 Jazz have been among the NBA's biggest disappointments this season. A lot of that has been the result of injuries, with Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen out now and Jusuf Nurkić having not yet debuted this season. The Jazz are painfully thin in the front court at this point, and the early partnership between Keyonte George and Darryn Peterson in the backcourt has yielded mixed results.

    Casting a wide net makes sense since the Jazz could theoretically use help basically anywhere. More of a playmaking guard to balance out the score-first instincts that George and Peterson bring would make sense. Wing depth, especially defense-first wing depth, would help address a major weakness. Dunn is a former Jazz player. And of course, adding some size to deal with all of those injuries would probably have the biggest immediate impact. Utah doesn't control its own first-round pick this year. The Jazz benefit from losing in no way, and that has seemingly made them eager to try to fight an uphill battle back into the Western Conference Play-In race.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, blake Griffin told an interesting story recently, recalling playing golf with former teammate JJ Redick. At that point, Redick was already retired and Griffin was nearing the end of his career.

    This was before Redick became the head coach of the Lakers. He had some perspective on his post-playing days that he offered to Griffin, something that stuck with the longtime Clipper years later. Redick told Griffin that he wouldn't be "truly happy" until he retired. Knowing how that might sound, Griffin was quick to clarify that they weren't miserable playing basketball, but rather that the two men were similar in their extensive, obsessive preparation.

    Sources indicate that "The way I took it and the way I think that he meant it," Griffin told GQ, "is it's such a grind, mental grind, physical grind of putting literally everything you have into this thing. And then when you're done, you just find this newly introduced sense of peace.".

    According to recent reports, put another way, pressure is baked into being in the NBA. The severity might vary from player to player or team to team, but it's natural enough to feel a certain amount of weight given the intensity of the competition. With that in mind, here are some estimations on current stress levels around the league.

    Recent findings suggest that all things considered, the Sixers have to be pretty happy with how they've started the season. Even after the Blazers snapped their five-game win streak on Monday, Philly is 14-4 and sits atop the East. LeBron James, unsurprisingly, has been a fantastic addition, particularly as a distributor and playmaker. Jaylen Brown is playing his usual heavy minutes while shooting nearly 50% from the floor. And, crucially, Joel Embiid — who missed a combined 150 games over the previous three seasons — has appeared in all but four games to date. Those are all wins for the Sixers.

    It has been revealed that to the extent that there's any cause for concern here, it's how sustainable all this is for them. Of the 18 games they've played, they're a perfect 12-0 in the clutch (games decided by five points or fewer with five minutes or less to go). That's tops in the NBA, and they must feel good about being at their best when things get a little dicey. But as Tyrese Maxey pointed out earlier in the season when they were starting to fall into this rhythm of playing close game after close game, he and the Sixers would prefer to stack a few victories that don't cause them to sweat right until the end.

    According to recent reports, winning in the clutch sure beats the alternative. For now, it's less of a problem than something to monitor.

    Just a couple of weeks ago, the Celtics won the battle of frenemies and were perched atop the Eastern Conference. Things haven't gone quite to proposal since then. All of a sudden, the Celtics have lost four in a row, including two one-point losses at Sacramento and Golden State. Boston handed the Kings just their second win of the season, and dropped the game to the Stephen Curry-less Warriors. Not the kind of basketball the Celtics are accustomed to playing.

    Things haven't been easy lately for Boston. The Sacramento and Golden State games were on a back-to-back as part of a difficult, still-in-progress stretch in the schedule in which Boston plays six of seven on the road, culminating in another back-to-back when the Celtics face the Spurs in San Antonio this coming Sunday, followed by the Mavericks in Dallas on Monday.

    It has been revealed that perhaps most troubling of all, two-way star Derrick White has been merely a one-way contributor for a while now. White had a disappointing shooting season a year ago. Considering his talent, the smart bet was that he would bounce back and be more efficient this season. That hasn't happened. White is shooting 41% from the floor and an abysmal 28.9% from deep. The 3-point mark is the worst of his career by a good stretch. He made just 2 of 12 from distance against the Warriors and was visibly frustrated with himself.

    Sources indicate that the Celtics have long had a theory of how they like to play: take and make more 3s than the opposition on any given night. When their shots are falling, they're tough to beat. When they aren't, anyone can knock them off. Right now, they're struggling, White in particular. Boston doesn't really have any choice but to let White try to shoot his way back into form. He's too key to their overall plans, and they'd never be able to replace his impact at the other end of the floor, where he remains one of the best all-around defenders in the league. Either he fixes his shot and Boston is back in business, or he doesn't and life at the office gets a lot tougher for everyone.

    When the Timberwolves announced in October that Anthony Edwards would undergo an arthroscopic procedure on his right knee, it took some people by surprise. Edwards looked good to start the season. He torched the Heat in the opening outing, going for 45 points and draining nine 3s. In his fourth game, on the second night of a back-to-back, he put up 47 points in a close two-point loss at Cleveland — and then suddenly and without warning, he was out of commission and expected to miss approximately two months.

    Industry observers note that edwards recently mentioned that he "never wanted to have surgery" and he felt pretty good during the offseason. He thought he was managing the knee well then, and it wasn't swollen during the summer. But after the aforementioned back-to-back, the knee "was really bad, like painful to fly. So I'm like, 'I'm gonna get [the surgery].'".

    Recent findings suggest that without him, the Wolves have fared better than some might have expected, going a tidy 10-4. They're third in the Western Conference, trailing only the Spurs and Lakers. That should have head coach Chris Finch and the Wolves optimistic about staying afloat until Edwards returns. Except no one seems to be sure when that might be, including Edwards, who recently cast some doubt on the initial timetable when he noted he has "no clue" when he'll be back on the floor.

    According to recent reports, if we go by the original estimation, two months would put Ant in late December. Now that ballpark appears far less than certain. The Wolves have performed admirably with him sidelined, but in a loaded West, Minnesota will need Edwards back sooner than "no clue" if it wants to stay near the top of the conference and especially if the Wolves hope to make a deep postseason run.

    It has been revealed that ant is the unquestionable leader in all departments for Minnesota. In his absence, things have sometimes felt a little tense  — to the point where one noted knucklehead has periodically gotten frustrated by another. Getting Edwards back would definitely help on the court. It wouldn't hurt the vibes, either.

    What are the Cavs even doing? They're 9-9 after losing to the Bulls (without Caleb Wilson, no less) on Monday. That puts them one game up on the Magic for seventh in the East. They're just 2-6 outside of Cleveland. But hey, James Harden recently went for 51 points against the Pacers and now has more 50-point games in his career than Kobe Bryant. Maybe that will console Cavs fans. Seems unlikely, though.

    When you reach the conference finals, bring back your four most important players and add a fifth starter coming off a promising season, the expectations are understandably high. So far, the Cavs haven't exactly met them. Cleveland has been a top 10 offensive team, but bottom 10 in defense. That leaves them pretty much looking like what their record indicates — average at best, a team that could lose to an inferior opponent (like, say, Chicago) on any random night in November.

    It certainly hasn't helped that they've been without Evan Mobley of late. He's missed the last six games with a toe injury. Peyton Watson, the aforementioned addition to the starting lineup, hasn't been anywhere near as good in Cleveland as he was in Denver last season. All of that has left Donovan Mitchell with too much heavy lifting, and so far he hasn't been able to shoulder the load on his own. The longer this mediocrity continues, the more we're left to wonder whether the Cavs are overdue to shake up their starting unit and offload one of the substantial names.

    [Looks around to see if anyone else is cringing] They just lost to the Pacers.

    Recent findings suggest that in fairness, no team has been hit with more major injuries than the Thunder. Jalen Williams (leg) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) could very well miss the remainder of the season after both underwent surgery, while Chet Holmgren (knee) is expected to miss at least three months. That's three of the team's five starters to begin the season. Not good. Except to hear the reigning back-to-back MVP tell it, there's something unexpected to be gleaned from the experience.

    "Honestly speaking, it's kind of fun," Shai Gilgeous-Alexander said last week. "We've kind of had the wind at our back the last couple of years and had our way a lot of nights, and to have that kind of adversity, it's kind of fun. I embrace it. It'll make me better.".

    SGA has a different definition of fun than most people. After losing in Indiana on Monday, the Thunder are just two games over .500, which puts them 10th in the West. [Go ahead and cringe if you weren't already doing so.].

    It has been revealed that if there's any team that can withstand SGA's bizarre version of a good time, it's the Thunder. Sam Presti assembled the deepest team in the NBA, but there are limits to what even they can handle. In the absence of several key players, Ajay Mitchell, Jared McCain, Isaiah Hartenstein and others have all been tasked with picking up considerable slack. That includes rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz. When you're missing so many important pieces, you stop being deep at some point and just do your best to plug holes. Even the mighty Thunder can only do so much.

    The Warriors snapped a five-game losing streak by beating the Celtics at home on Sunday in a white-knuckled one-point win. Alas, they only managed 88 points in the victory and the offense looked super sluggish yet again. Even with the win over Boston, the Warriors are 9-8 and 11th in the West standings. Things have gone sideways when you're looking up at everyone but the Pelicans, Clippers, Jazz and Kings.

    According to recent reports, the Warriors' start to the season was fun while it lasted. Yaxel Lendeborg played great — and talked just as well — and immediately cemented himself in the starting lineup, not to mention the Rookie of the Year race. Even more encouraging, Stephen Curry looked like a vintage version of himself again after playing just 43 games a season ago. Through the first 11 games this year, Curry was second in the league in scoring behind only Luka Dončić. He appeared sharp and healthy — until he came out of the game in Houston in early November while holding his side after playing just six minutes. Turned out to be an abdominal tear. The Warriors announced that he would be reevaluated in two weeks, though the general ballpark for that kind of injury is closer to a month.

    In a recent development, not great, especially considering the Warriors were hardly at full strength as it was. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody have yet to play a single minute while both recover from knee injuries. Meanwhile, Kristaps Porziņģis — who signed a newly introduced two-year deal worth $40 million in the offseason — is dealing with health issues and recently stepped away from basketball. Curry is the most critical piece of all, but not having several key components has left the Warriors painfully thin. That has reminded the Warriors how much tougher life is for all of them when Curry isn't on the floor and a rookie is suddenly tasked with leading the way.

    Recent findings suggest that the recently ended losing streak included a stretch at San Antonio, Upcoming Orleans, Dallas and Memphis during which the average margin of defeat was more than 27 points. The loss to the Spurs was bad enough that Lendeborg came back with a new cut, prompting Steve Kerr to quip that the rookie dealt with the defeat by "[chopping] all his hair off.".

    It has been revealed that through it all, Draymond hasn't been able to stop being Draymond. Green spent the run-up to the Celtics meeting warring with an NBA unc online, then got called for a tech while sitting on the bench during the game. Take a breath and go for a walk, man.

    Curry can't return soon enough. If this goes on much longer, Yaxel and the rest of them will be fully bald.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Jacksonville Jaguars will be without at least two of their most important playmakers when they host the Tennessee Titans this Sunday. Star wideout Parker Washington and lead running back Bhayshul Tuten have been ruled out for Week 12 against the Tennessee Titans.

    In a recent development, washington was ruled out after suffering a shoulder injury during Thursday's practice session, according to a report from ESPN. Head coach Liam Coen stated Washington is considered week-to-week. Tuten has been dealing with an ankle injury aggravated in Week 11; he was listed as out on Friday's injury report.

    Washington is the Jaguars' leading receiver this season, with 44 catches for 748 yards and six touchdowns through 10 games. He's less than 100 receiving yards away from a new career high, and his 17.0 yards per reception presently rank fifth in the NFL. The former sixth-round pick out of Penn State is coming off two straight 100-yard performances. He caught eight passes for 103 yards against the New York Giants last Sunday, and seven passes for 152 yards and a touchdown against the Titans in Week 10.

    It has been revealed that with Washington out of the lineup for at least one week, Trevor Lawrence will look to utilize Jakobi Meyers, Josh Cameron, and Brian Thomas Jr. more in the passing game. Meyers is Jacksonville's second-leading receiver with 493 yards on 33 receptions.

    Tuten has been the lead back on a Jaguars rushing offense that ranks 10th in the league in EPA per carry and ninth in yards after contact over expected, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. The second-year back has already either set or matched career highs in rushing yards (642), receiving yards (226), rushing touchdowns (5), and receiving touchdowns (3) just 10 games into the season.

    It has been revealed that as for Tuten's replacement, Chris Rodriguez Jr. and Ameer Abdullah could see more work on Sunday.

    In a recent development, the Jaguars had no problem with the Titans in their first matchup this season, defeating Tennessee 40-23 just two weeks ago. However, Washington becomes a crucial piece for a Jaguars team looking to make a serious playoff push. The Jaguars could still be without Washington as their schedule ramps up, with road games against the Chicago Bears and Houston Texans in two of the next three weeks.

    While Jacksonville at the moment has a 94.3% chance to win their division, according to CBS Sports Forecasting & Projections, the Jaguars need to keep winning to maximize their postseason chances. Jacksonville is averaging more points per game (28.7) than any team in franchise history and entered Week 12 with the league's best points-per-game differential (+12.0). However, currently sitting at 7-3 behind the Denver Broncos and tied with the Cincinnati Bengals, the Jaguars hope to avoid a fourth-seed finish and a potential wild-card matchup with either the Broncos or the Kansas City Chiefs. Jacksonville dropped their Week 2 matchup against the Broncos, while they narrowly beat the Chiefs in Week 5 of 2025.

    Industry News: Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • According to recent reports, tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short.
    • Sources indicate that christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    According to recent reports, tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX).

    Sources indicate that christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

    Sources indicate that on the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

    Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 Pressing System.

    The Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

    According to recent reports, A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

    The attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim demonstrated some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The concern, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

    Tottenham’s Width-Based Strategy.

    Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

    Industry observers note that the half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

    Sources indicate that hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

    Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

    In general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, demonstrated excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He quickly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

    Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses.

    According to recent reports, A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

    Recent findings suggest that due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too swiftly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

    Overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

    Sources indicate that an additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant complications in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

    2-0 and 50% Possession at Halftime.

    By the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate new build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

    According to recent reports, additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

    Despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham revealed general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

    Through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

    In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game blueprint was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

    In principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

    The extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

    Industry observers note that the central problem with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

    It has been revealed that both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

    Industry observers note that in general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

    Sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

    Towards the end of the half, Hoffenheim shifted its strategic focus from long balls to short build-up plays, which were mainly initiated on the right side. Kadeřábek positioned himself increasingly wide, which proved effective, as his direct opponent Son, starting from a half-space position, had to cover a long pressing distance and often arrived too late. This allowed Kadeřábek to receive the ball.

    From there, Hoffenheim attempted to play rapidly into depth to Hložek or Becker. However, Tottenham effectively defended this option through consistent man-marking. Becker’s dropping movements were frequently neutralized by Maddison’s covering shadow in the half-space, while Stach was largely covered by Richarlison, limiting the connections into the center significantly.

    In the second half, Hoffenheim continued with this approach, but increasingly operated from a 2-3-4-1 formation, while Tottenham defended in a 4-1-4-1. The full-backs positioned themselves in extreme width early in the build-up phases to maximize the pressing distances of their direct opponents. This approach remained effective: With clean first touches, Hoffenheim occasionally managed to beat their opponents with dribbles.

    The biggest difference from the first half lay in the subsequent movements from wide positions. Unlike in the first half, Hoffenheim refrained from structurally overloading the last line. The focus shifted towards deeper positioning to create diagonal passing options. This allowed Hoffenheim to either play directly behind Tottenham’s defensive line or use the space in between, where Hložek was frequently available for a pass.

    According to recent reports, there were also frequent rotations, for example between Bischof and Becker, which created additional dynamism. Kramaric often dropped into the defensive midfield space, allowing for the resolution of the isolation of that space by Richarlison, as Tottenham didn’t follow these wide runs in their man-marking system. This allowed Kramaric to distribute the ball on several occasions.

    Industry observers note that A positive aspect was that Akpoguma kept up with Kadeřábek’s wide movements, constantly offering a return pass option. Meanwhile, Stach often dropped deeper to cover space for counter-attacks—a lesson learned from the first half. Since Tottenham struggled to defend the width consistently, the pressing became deeper, and Hoffenheim’s pressure steadily increased.

    Although Hoffenheim almost completely stopped playing long balls, the wide fullbacks presented themselves as viable options for diagonal switches, which were frequently sought. Sometimes Bischof also dropped wide to be available for these passes. These passes were mostly successful, as they were played into open spaces rather than into congested areas. Moreover, the 2-3-4-1 formation allowed for much better access to second balls due to the increased midfield presence.

    Recent findings suggest that for Tottenham, however, it remained a similar game to the first half. They still faced significant problems with the opponent behind them and technical difficulties in their ball retention play. Solanke added a bit more depth in the forward position, while Moore displayed more dribbling strength on the left wing. Despite some good individual actions, the problem areas—particularly in the final third from the very static 2-3-5—were still largely unresolved. Hoffenheim, on the other hand, simply had a better ball possession structure and dominated the game with nearly 61% possession. The counter-pressing challenges ultimately led to Hoffenheim’s 1-2 goal.

    In a recent development, towards the end of the match, Ilzer switched to a 2-4-4 system with double-wide wingers, while Spurs also switched to a 4-1-4-1 formation, defending much wider. They tried to directly cut off the connection to the wide fullbacks, which they succeeded in doing effectively. Once they were bypassed, however, the fullbacks advanced well. The central players were now more tightly marked, following movements towards the ball. It wasn’t until Moore failed to notice Kadeřábek’s off-the-ball runs in the 88th minute that Hoffenheim managed to break free on the wing and score the 2-3 goal.

    Overall, Tottenham’s initially wider setup made the half-space more accessible, which Hoffenheim repeatedly attempted to exploit. However, Moerstedt and Kramaric found few solutions against Tottenham’s well-defending center-backs. Several of these situations led to relieving counter-attacks for Tottenham, which were also the most dangerous for them in the second half. Especially towards the end of the match, as Solanke and Lankshear pressed for ball recoveries, Tottenham could quickly play vertically forward after regaining possession. Maddison’s dribbling pace was also frequently on display in these moments. It was clear that the fact Tottenham was ahead and Hoffenheim needed to win played into their hands.

    Recent findings suggest that the conclusion is ambivalent. Both teams are going through a difficult phase, which was reflected in the match—many fouls, turnovers, and long balls shaped the game. It was not a particularly convincing display from two teams that, in terms of personnel and concept, should be doing better. Both sides were often forced into wide areas or specific zones, which fragmented the combination play in the final third and lacked the necessary dynamism.

    According to recent reports, however, there were still glimpses of solid, familiar approaches, particularly from Hoffenheim, though the team still lacks the presence and stability required to compete against stronger opponents. As Ilzer highlighted in the post-match press conference: “We’ve learned that we need to be more stable to get the right results. In duels man against man, we lacked something. Still, you can see we can play really good football. We ruin a good game for ourselves when we make such simple mistakes. It was too easy for the opponent.”.

    Postecoglou’s team also showed deficiencies, especially in ball movement, presence in the final third, and intensity without the ball. Ultimately, the team that managed to relieve pressure better came out on top, while the other, had they played the second half like the first, might have seen a different outcome.

    MX flirted with the RB school but secretly remained a romantic when it came to Guardiola’s football artistry. He is right now working as an analyst at a youth academy and is also an author for ‘spielverlagerung next generation.’.

    #166264. NBA Hater Report: Celtics can't shoot, neither can Trae Young and James Harden isn't close to a top 10 player

    NBA Hater Report: Celtics can't shoot, neither can Trae Young and James Harden isn't close to a top 10 player

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2152 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly.
    • The Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors.
    • Recent findings suggest that lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that welcome back to the NBA Hater Report: A breakdown of some of the players, teams and trends around the league that are drawing the ire of yours truly. If you're not a fellow pessimist, proceed with caution.

    The Celtics are hitting their first skid of the season, having lost four straight to drop to 11-6, including a demoralizing back-to-back against the now two-win Kings and the sans-Stephen Curry Warriors. They failed to hit 100 points against the Kings and their 28th-ranked defense. They managed just 87 at Golden State.

    Recent findings suggest that lack of rim pressure was always going to be, and has long been, an obstacle for the Celtics, who are averaging just 47 drives per game (third-fewest in the league). Only 25.6% of their shots are at the rim, the fourth-fewest in the league per Cleaning the Glass, and no team takes fewer shots per game from inside the restricted area.

    They are about as extreme a jump-shooting team as you will find, and right now the shots are not going in. Over these last four, the Celtics have made just 28% of their 3s and 38% of their overall shots. Throw in 65% from the free-throw line and those are all bottom-two marks over that span, plus the 389 points they scored is the lowest over any four-game stretch since 2012 for a Boston offense.

    It's not just the number of 3s the Celtics rely, sometimes more than others, it's the kinds of 3s. Every team wants the shots off ball and player movement, drives and kicks, drawing two and swinging, but when the Celtics aren't able to create the initial leverage by attacking the rim (they don't have to do this with just drives; they aim to do so by cutting and rolling, too), they end up taking more pull-up 3s than any team in the league, both as a total number and percentage of their overall shot diet.

    Recent findings suggest that those are traditionally tougher shots, and indeed Boston is making them at a 33.5% clip. The Celtics also don't generate a ton of the coveted corner 3s (which are often a result of rim pressure) relative to their volume, and thus take more above-the-break 3s than any team. There are also a lot of one-on-one 3s; only the Lakers and Timberwolves take more 3s after three or more dribbles, and the Celtics make those at only 29%.

    According to recent reports, bottom line, Derrick White is shooting 28% from 3 for the year and has missed 22 of his last 25 from deep (he had so many premium looks against Golden State and they just will not go in for him). Payton Pritchard has missed 21 of his last 29 from deep. Jayson Tatum is having a stellar all-around season and is leveraging his scoring attention to find teammates more effectively than ever, but quietly his shooting is in the dumps, too.

    Tatum is shooting 42.6% overall and 33.6% from 3, both of which would be career lows if you discard the 15 games he played last season after returning ahead of schedule from the Achilles tear. Tatum has never been a particularly adept pull-up 3-point shooter, for which he'll probably always be prone to settling to at least some degree. Tatum's pull-up 3s over his last four full seasons:.

    According to recent reports, any team that debuts as many 3s as the Celtics is going to endure some extreme ebbs and flows, and coach Joe Mazzulla remains committed to the course. "... If we're getting good shots, which more times than not we are, you have to be able to trust over the course of a season that that's going to work out," he noted.

    Sources indicate that the truth is, the Celtics don't really have a choice other than to trust the shots to go in. They don't have a proposal B to speak of. They don't get to the rim and they don't have a post presence. They have a gang of good shooters, but that doesn't guarantee good shooting.

    In a recent development, the Celtics rely on getting more shots than their opponents by winning the turnover and offensive-rebounding battles, which they generally do, but as Mazzulla also stated, "at some point you have to knock [the shots] down. That's just not happening right now.".

    After Harden scored 51 against the Pacers last Friday, Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson did the increasingly cliché "we've got to appreciate this guy" dance while calling Harden a "top 10 of all-time" player.

    Industry observers note that kenny Atkinson after James Harden's 51-point game: "We've got to appreciate this guy. This guy is top 10 of all-time." pic.twitter.com/YUt2Y6pQYL.

    According to recent reports, remember, Atkinson is the guy who told reporters: "Analytically … we've won two out of three" right before the Cavaliers got swept by the Knicks in last year's Eastern Conference Finals. That was kind of overblown, to be fair. He was simply citing the types of shots the Cavs got vs. the ones the Knicks got, and that getting the right shots is a recipe for success more often than not, which every coach from the beginning of time has believed.

    Industry observers note that atkinson just would've been better off if he'd gone the "make or miss league" route. Once you start invoking analytical results over actual results, you're going to get rightfully roasted as the number nerd that you are.

    In a recent development, through this lens, it makes sense that Atkinson thinks Harden is a top 10 all-time player. Numbers-wise, he's ninth all-time with almost 30,000 career points. He's 11th in assists and, barring injury, will almost surely pass Isiah Thomas for 10th by the end of the season. Only Stephen Curry has made more 3-pointers than Harden, who's piled up so many numbers he's actually top 20 all-time in steals.

    None of this adds up to top 10.

    Of course this is subjective, but this is my Hater Report, so allow me to hate. Harden was a manipulating machine of egregious proportions. I'm not saying he wasn't a great scorer, or even that he sometimes still isn't. Two things can indeed be true. But if we're going to start throwing around top 10, we're sure as hell going to factor heavily the conditions under which you dominated.

    According to recent reports, harden played in the NBA's version of the steroid era. It was juiced up on some level for every scorer, but nobody mastered the dark arts like Harden, who cheated his way to so many phony fouls that guys were literally starting to guard him with their hands behind their backs.

    Now listen, before you start with the "he wasn't breaking any rules" nonsense, keep in mind that steroids weren't technically illegal in baseball when Barry Bonds' head looked like it was going to pop. Harden scammed his way to more points than anyone in history. The flops and flails were impossible to stomach or, more importantly, defend against. Falling down on damn near every 3-pointer he took actually became part of his follow-through. I would only be mildly surprised if you hid a camera in his private workouts if he wasn't falling down in an empty gym, because he was so used to doing it.

    This created more than just a gazillion free throws; it created a scoring environment in which Harden could operate against defenders who were way more frightened of fouling than being scored on. It was as if he was being perpetually defended by guys with five fouls.

    Now account for the one-man-show usage. I remember Raja Bell once telling me there are way more players than you think who could score 25 points per game if given the opportunity. Hell, Darius Acuff Jr. is doing it right now and until a week ago, he was a teenager.

    That's not to say anyone could do what Harden did, but given his set of circumstances, it's irresponsible to call him one of the 10 greatest players ever on numbers alone. Back in 2022, ESPN ranked him 50th all time, which feels much closer to reality, and he's only gotten worse since then.

    I mean, just start rattling names off the top of your head. Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant, Wilt Chamberlain, Larry Bird, Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Hakeem Olajuwon, Kobe Bryant, Tim Duncan, Shaquille O'Neal. We're already at 12 and there's not even a debate with any of them.

    No coach in his right mind would take Harden over Nikola Jokić, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Kevin Garnett, Karl Malone, Scottie Pippen, Charles Barkley, Isiah Thomas, Dwyane Wade or prime Chris Paul. I never watched Oscar Robertson, Jerry West, Julius Erving, Moses Malone, Elgin Baylor or some guy named Bill Russell, but something tells me the vast majority of coaches are taking those guys over Harden, too.

    It bears repeating that none of this means to suggest Harden hasn't been an all-time player. He's a first-ballot Hall of Famer. He's not an empty-stats guy by any stretch; he led a team that very possibly would've won the championship in the middle of Golden State's dynasty were it not for a Chris Paul injury. But there are levels to this, and trying to elevate Harden into the top one on the strength of gaudy numbers in an absolutely juiced-up era of his game would be like trying to call Sammy Sosa one of the greatest hitters ever. It's just not even close to true.

    Recent findings suggest that back in 2021, I called Young an average shooter who thinks he's Stephen Curry and got absolutely roasted for it. Turns out, I wasn't harsh enough on Young, whose shooting has been consistently deteriorating to the point that he is now a flat-out bad shooter. Even with a 7-for-15 run from 3 over his last two games, which at this point is a downright nuclear stretch for him, Young is shooting 32.5% from 3 and a pitiful 36.4% overall.

    Recent findings suggest that the fact that he's among the league leaders in assists means almost nothing; passing has always been his one elite gift (it goes largely hand in hand with his former ability to breach the paint at will), but it comes at the hefty cost of him controlling the ball for almost the same amount of time per possession as Luka Dončić this season. Just because those two were traded for one another doesn't mean they are, or ever have been, anywhere near the same caliber of player.

    Recent findings suggest that even at his peak when he was one of the league's better shot generators, it was debatable whether you could justify sponsoring Young's personal dribbling show with your offense, let alone paying him max money given the defensive trade-off. But now that he can't shoot or beat anyone off the dribble, that $212 million deal the Wizards gifted him this summer, which was a disaster the moment the ink dried, somehow looks even worse.

    Washington is trying to salvage some sort of value from Young. They're starting to take him off the ball some, which, given the good shooting the last few games, is going to give the apologists hope. Don't fall for it. The numbers, not just this year but going back a long time, speak for themselves.

    According to recent reports, there's a difference between a talented shooter and a good one. Young fooled people with range and confidence for a while, and he had an unearned marksman reputation that died hard. But the jig is up. This is an average shooter at best, and he's rarely at his best.

    After losing four straight games by 20-plus while also being held under 100 points in each (an equation of futility that goes unmatched by any other team this century), the Warriors finally got their first win since losing Curry to an oblique tear by beating the aforementioned ice-cold Celtics.

    According to recent reports, it certainly wasn't because of their offense. The Warriors were once again held to double digits, managing just 88 points. Over this five-game stretch, the Warriors, who register a top-five offense with Curry, have scraped together an anemic 96.2 points per 100 possessions on 48.5% true-shooting, both being the worst marks in the league by a laughable margin.

    Over this five-game stretch, the Warriors have been outscored by 108 points. The 1997-98 team that also lost four straight by at least 20 points was a minus-104 over that stretch. That was the season that Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo, mind you. The Warriors won 19 games. That's the kind of organization these Warriors are trolling in right now.

    If Curry doesn't get back soon, we might have to start worrying about Draymond Green putting Steve Kerr in a full nelson.

    Tech Report: Dylan Larkin trade grades: Red Wings notch massive win in blockbuster NHL deal with Canadiens

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Detroit Red Wings have traded former captain Dylan Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a blockbuster trade, the teams announced on Sunday.
    • Industry observers note that in addition to Larkin, Detroit sent a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Montreal.
    • Larkin requested a trade back in June, and his relationship with the Red Wings only grew more acrimonious with each passing day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Detroit Red Wings have traded former captain Dylan Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens in a blockbuster trade, the teams announced on Sunday. This deal ends a bitter saga between Larkin and the Red Wings, and Montreal gave up a king's ransom to make it happen.

    Industry observers note that in addition to Larkin, Detroit sent a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Montreal. The Red Wings received forward Kirby Dach, goaltender Sam Montembeault, prospect Michael Hage, first-round picks in 2027 and 2029, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fourth-round pick.

    Larkin requested a trade back in June, and his relationship with the Red Wings only grew more acrimonious with each passing day. As training camp opened in September, Detroit revealed that Larkin had been stripped of his captaincy, and Larkin was booed by fans on opening night at Little Caesars Arena.

    After recovering from an injury he suffered in camp, Larkin played 10 games before announcing that he would be sitting out in anticipation of the trade. While sitting out, Larkin racked up major fines, but his trade request has finally been granted.

    According to recent reports, when he's on the ice, there's no denying that Larkin can make a significant impact. The 30-year-old Larkin just notched 34 goals and 33 assists for the Red Wings last season -- his fifth straight year hitting the 30-goal mark -- and he was instrumental in Team USA ending its lengthy gold medal drought at the 2026 Olympics.

    In his career, Larkin has totaled 278 goals and 371 assists in 818 games. The first game Larkin — a native of Waterford, Michigan — plays for the Habs will also be the first he's ever played for a team based outside the Wolverine State.

    Larkin will give the Canadiens much-needed center depth, and he'll be under contract for a while. He's in the fourth year of an eight-year contract that pays him $8.7 million per season.

    This trade fills a void that's existed in the Canadiens' lineup for several years now. Nick Suzuki has evolved into a legitimate star and a franchise-caliber No. 1 center. Beyond him, Montreal has struggled to find a true second-line center.

    Industry observers note that larkin absolutely fits that bill. While he was a bit miscast in Detroit as a first-line center, Larkin is one of the best No. 2 options in the NHL, and he gives the Canadiens an elite one-two punch down the middle.

    Did the Canadiens overpay a bit for a 30-year-old second-line center? In a vacuum, they did. However, taken in context, this deal makes plenty of sense for the Habs.

    Sources indicate that montreal's championship window is just now opening. It already has an elite young core locked up for the next several seasons on team-friendly deals. Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Ivan Demidov, Juraj Slafkovsky, Lane Hutson and Noah Dobson are all 27 or younger and make less than $10 million per season.

    Sources indicate that that gives general manager Kent Hughes a bit more freedom to be aggressive on the trade market. Picks and prospects are nice, but they don't do much good for a team looking to make the jump to contender status in 2026-27. Besides, the Canadiens have been building their prospect pool for years now. It's time to flip some of those assets for proven star power.

    The Canadiens paid a premium to acquire Larkin. There's no two ways about it. However, Montreal fills a major need and looks a lot more formidable in the Eastern Conference. The Stanley Cup window is officially wide open for the ascending Canadiens. Grade -- B+.

    Consider the situation interim general manager Shawn Horcoff faced. Everyone knew that Larkin wanted out of Detroit so badly that he was paying not to play for the Red Wings.

    On top of that, Larkin had a full no-trade clause, and his list of approved teams amounted to no more than a dozen.

    Should I also mention that Horcoff was thrust into this role in the midst of the offseason, when franchise legend Steve Yzerman was effectively fired for mishandling the Wings' rebuild?

    Given all of that, it's hard to see this as anything less than a home run for Detroit. In fact, it's probably more like a grand slam. Not only did the Red Wings get multiple first-round picks and a couple useful NHL players out of the deal, but they also landed a legitimate blue-chip prospect in Hage.

    Recent findings suggest that the No. 21 pick in the 2024 NHL Draft, Hage is off to a roaring start at the University of Michigan this season with five goals and 21 assists in just 13 games. Detroit might have replaced one franchise center with another one, assuming Hage continues to develop at this rate.

    This was a great piece of work from Horcoff, who probably just made a strong case for the full-time general manager gig in Detroit. This haul will allow the Wings to kickstart another retool or swing a significant trade to bolster the current roster. Either way, the outlook just got a lot brighter in Hockeytown. Grade -- A+.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

    Published: 12:00 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 12:02 EST, 23 November 2026.

    Chelsea are lurching towards a crisis after yet another loss in which they were bullied, this time by Leeds United.

    That 4-1 hiding saw Xabi Alonso heckled, and his players booed at both half-time and full-time, arguably deservedly so for such a disastrous showing.

    It has led to tentative speculation around Alonso's future as Chelsea prepare to travel to Oliver Glasner's Nottingham Forest on Friday night, not to mention questions about where he is going wrong and how he might arrest his team's slump in form.

    Here, Daily Mail Sport tackles all the burning issues at Stamford Bridge...

    Recent findings suggest that chief among Chelsea’s problems is the fact they have conceded 20 Premier League goals this season. It is as many as they have scored at the other end. So, as much as we have enjoyed their freescoring forward line this season, so too must we criticise their disastrous defending.

    According to recent reports, we know Alonso can organise a defence. His Bayer Leverkusen side only conceded 24 goals when they won the Bundesliga as unbeaten champions in 2023-24. Chelsea are now on the verge of overtaking that total before we even hit December.

    Liam Delap, their former striker now at Forest, will be desperate to add to that tally this Friday, too.

    Xabi Alonso is coming under growing pressure, with his Chelsea side failing to back up their promising early-season form.

    Levi Colwill was all at sea against Leeds as Chelsea shipped another four goals, taking their tally to 20 in 11 games.

    Recent findings suggest that this morning, I watched back all 20 of the goals that Chelsea have leaked this term. There have been so many individual mistakes.

    Like on day one, in the 3-2 win at Fulham, when an out of position Robert Sanchez let in Josh King's shot. And when Levi Colwill missed a defensive header which should have been routine, which led to Gonzalo Garcia scoring.

    Chelsea got rid of Sanchez after that game, but Emiliano Martinez has hardly helped shore up this defence, as was apparent in the 4-1 loss to Leeds, when Colwill and Co were again all over the shop.

    Until they cut out the silly mistakes, it is hard to see Chelsea competing at the top end of the Premier League.

    Every manager at every club is sackable. Nobody is immune. But that’s not to say Alonso is suddenly up for the chop at Chelsea. I haven’t heard anything which would suggest those inside the club think finding a fourth permanent manager in the year 2026 is the answer.

    Let’s not forget the overwhelming optimism when news broke of Chelsea striking an agreement to hire Alonso. It was an hour or so after the club had lost the 2026 FA Cup final to Manchester City. Recently, I took a look at the comments section of the story I wrote that day. It was full of excitement from Chelsea fans, and anger from Liverpool supporters at missing out on him.

    Industry observers note that anyway, I think it’s too soon for us to start talking about Alonso’s job. He is in a bad moment, obviously. A very bad moment. Losing at home to Tottenham Hotspur and Leeds is a complete no-no for any Blues boss.

    The supporters are more likely to curse his name than chant it right now, and it is hard to identify the style Alonso wants, with few discernible patterns of play to Chelsea's football.

    But let’s give the bloke a chance to get himself out of this jam as he heads into his 12th Premier League match.

    In a recent development, believe it or not, Chelsea don’t like changing managers mid-season if they can help it. Enzo Maresca resigned, exiting on January 1, 2026. Liam Rosenior was sacked, yes, but the club were effectively forced into that change as the players clearly gave up on him. Let’s see if Alonso can find some solutions.

    Chelsea don’t like changing managers mid-season if they can help it and Alonso, remember, has only had 11 Premier League games in charge.

    We’ve tried to coax a little anger out of Alonso at press conferences, practically encouraging him to have a pop at his players for how they are performing, but he tends to resist the urge.

    Industry observers note that he’s clearly a nice guy. However, a Chelsea source does tell me he’s different behind the scenes. We may not see it on the outside, but internally, he is perfectly capable of being fiery with the players.

    In a recent development, which I hope is the case. Because sometimes, it can feel as if these Chelsea players need a good kick up the backside, rather than being coddled.

    I wrote a piece after the 4-1 loss to Leeds about how superstars can be stroppy. It’s normal. They can be so good that when the game isn’t going their way, they show their sulky side.

    Recent findings suggest that palmer did that both during and after Saturday’s defeat. It was pretty poor from him to not want to go around applauding the fans who had bothered to stick around at full-time, even if there had been boos. An apology has been attributed to Palmer on social media, but that’s just another case of fake quotes being circulated.

    According to recent reports, for me, Palmer has to look at himself as much as anybody. It’s been too long since we’ve seen him try to take a match by the scruff of the neck.

    Cole Palmer put in another quiet display against Leeds - he needs to start taking matches by the scruff of the neck.

    WHAT HAPPENED WITH EMEGHA AFTER THE GAME?

    Sources indicate that striker Emmanuel Emegha started for the first time and scored for the first time in Chelsea’s 4-1 loss to Leeds. Then he exited Stamford Bridge.

    We have seen players leaving the stadium on foot before. Videos of Palmer being surrounded by supporters while being escorted to his ride home occasionally crop up on social media.

    Emegha had possessions stolen from his car while he was in a restaurant after the match and the incident has been reported to police. He was not harmed.

    From a footballing point of view, I'd like to see Emegha start away at Forest this Friday.

    It has been revealed that not that I’m aware. He’s been linked with Paris Saint-Germain and I had an email from a PR person this morning trying to push a loan to AC Milan or Roma as a possibility.

    Alonso has given the fans what they wanted in the last few league games. He started Estevao against Manchester United, brought him on at half-time at Sunderland and started him against Leeds.

    Estevao, clearly an exciting talent, could do with taking these opportunities to show why he deserves more of them.

    Estevao has been given a chance to shine by Alonso in recent weeks but has failed to grab his opportunities.

    I could see Malo Gusto leaving if there’s interest and Chelsea don’t keep demanding £75million, because it is hard to see who would spend that on him.

    Sources indicate that gusto started in five of Alonso’s first six games in all competitions at the beginning of the campaign. Since then, he has been handed one start in eight, and that was in the Carabao Cup at Liverpool. Coming on as a substitute in the loss to Leeds, he tried and failed to play Brenden Aaronson offside and was then beaten by his man as the visitors made it 4-1.

    I wouldn’t be surprised if a few other fringe players are linked with leaving in pursuit of game time ahead of January, such as Valentin Barco and Jamie Gittens, who is training again after his ankle injury.

    Industry observers note that as for incomings, I don’t need to tell you that Chelsea are interested in Alex Scott of Bournemouth. Arsenal are, too, but the word is the Blues are still the frontrunners as we approach January. Whether Scott is what this team needs is another conversation.

    #166260. A premature, unauthorized, tiered ranking of every possible Dallas Cowboys coach -- should Jerry Jones need it
