    A premature, unauthorized, tiered ranking of every possible Dallas Cowboys coach -- should Jerry Jones need it

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the Dallas Cowboys are a disaster.
    • Sources indicate that they have suffered several embarrassing defeats this season, including two in which they blew multi-score fourth-quarter leads at home and two in which they lost to backup quarterbacks — again at home.
    • It should also probably be the nail in the coffin for head coach Brian Schottenheimer, who is clearly in over his head and who even Jerry Jones has admitted is learning on the job as a head coach and may not get to where he needs to to find success for years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the Dallas Cowboys are a disaster. After their latest calamitous loss, the Cowboys are 5-7 and their playoff "hopes" barely exist anymore.

    Sources indicate that they have suffered several embarrassing defeats this season, including two in which they blew multi-score fourth-quarter leads at home and two in which they lost to backup quarterbacks — again at home. The Thanksgiving loss to the division rival Philadelphia Eagles, of course, qualifies for both of those lists and is presumably the nail in the coffin for their season.

    It should also probably be the nail in the coffin for head coach Brian Schottenheimer, who is clearly in over his head and who even Jerry Jones has admitted is learning on the job as a head coach and may not get to where he needs to to find success for years. Jones has stated several times that he is not considering a change at head coach and that he still feels that Schottenheimer is the right man for the job. But he should be considering a change, and he's pretty clearly wrong about Schottenheimer, who has shown in two seasons that he is not a difference-making coach — at least not in a good way.

    It's probably time, then, to think about what might come next in Dallas. Jones is extremely reluctant to admit he's wrong and fire his hand-picked coaches — he let Jason Garrett and Mike McCarthy's contracts expire rather than fire them. He's even more reluctant to pay multiple coaches at once. And he's somehow even more reluctant than that to pay what it takes to land the best coaches on the market.

    For some context: The Cowboys have only interviewed six coaches in total over the last two times they had an opening, and they basically rigged the processes for McCarthy and Schottenheimer. But that shouldn't stop us from thinking about who might be available, and how they might fit in Dallas.

    That's why we're here: to speculate wildly about all the possible candidates for the Cowboys job, should it come open at some point. We're breaking things down by category and including every name we can think of that qualifies for each. Plenty of these potential hires don't make much sense, but Jones' past hires haven't made much sense either, so that shouldn't be disqualifying.

    North Carolina HC Bill Belichick.

    Let's be very, very clear: Neither of these hires would be a good idea.

    Sources indicate that saban has been out of coaching entirely for several years and out of the NFL since a wildly unsuccessful tenure with the Miami Dolphins came to a close in 2006. He now spends most of his time shilling for SEC schools and the College Sports Protection Act on ESPN's College GameDay. The only reason to hire him would be that he is Nick Saban.

    The end of Belichick's run with the Fresh England Patriots was not great. His time with the Tar Heels has been largely unsuccessful so far, with a losing record in each season and scandal(s) off the field. He used to be the Super Bowl-winning Bill Belichick, though, so Jones could be enticed by the idea of bringing him in.

    Tomlin is probably going to be the hottest candidate on the market this offseason, given his success in Pittsburgh. He's certainly a high-floor candidate, having shown the ability to rack up winning seasons, but he's probably not a particularly high-ceiling candidate, given he hasn't won a playoff game since 2016. He also hasn't shown much ability to identify good play-calling assistants on either side of the ball (Tomlin himself doesn't call plays).

    Industry observers note that still, he's probably the safest potential hire on the board, and it would come with a lot of good press. Most of the credit for any wins in the future would go to Tomlin and not Jones, though, so I'd consider this one unlikely given Jerry's track record of wanting credit for everything.

    Industry observers note that mcDermott is a similarly high-floor candidate. He showed the ability to rack up winning seasons in Buffalo — and not just when Josh Allen was his quarterback — the Bills went to the playoffs with Tyrod Taylor in 2017. McDermott's defenses during his time with the Bills were generally good but also not quite good enough when playoff time rolled around. He also was among the more conservative coaches when it came to game management, which isn't ideal in the modern NFL. But if you're looking for a safe hire, you could certainly do worse than McDermott, who has had a lot of success.

    Industry observers note that the only reason Shanahan is even being mentioned here is that he's who Troy Aikman has noted he'd hire as his head coach if he ever got the opportunity, and a potential marriage between Aikman and the Cowboys has been floated several times this year. The 49ers are never going to agree to trade Shanahan, though, and certainly not to the Cowboys. That's why this section is titled "never-happening trade candidates" and not just "trade candidates.".

    According to recent reports, each of these coaches' teams has been disappointing this season, and at this point it wouldn't be that surprising if they weren't asked back for another year. Ryan has shown the ability to coach a top defense, which the Cowboys obviously desperately need. Steichen has coaxed top offenses out of questionable quarterback play before and could do good work with Dak Prescott. Moore was seemingly Jones' anointed successor to Mike McCarthy before that relationship blew up.

    Oklahoma Sooners Interim OC Jason Witten.

    Colorado Buffaloes HC Deion Sanders.

    It has been revealed that witten might be the single-most likely candidate on this list to actually get the job, given his pedigree. He's a Cowboys legend. Jones loves him and has been praising him as a future NFL head coach for years. It would basically be like hiring Jason Garrett, but if the player was actually good when he was on the Cowboys. (That's not a comment on Witten's coaching acumen — just on Jones' thought process when it comes to hiring coaches.) Oklahoma's offense has actually improved since Witten took over play-calling duties, so maybe there is something there, but most of his success has come at the high school level.

    Sources indicate that sanders is another former Cowboys player and a hire that would generate a massive amount of attention. Considering how his tenure in Colorado has gone since his team lost Travis Hunter and Shedeur Sanders, though, it's probably not a hire that would generate much enthusiasm. Still, Jerry loves a story, and Deion in Dallas would be arguably the biggest story out there.

    Adams is highly respected, has shown the ability to design a good run game in both Dallas and Arizona, would probably come cheaply (which is important for Jones, as we know) and is right down the hall, which is where the Cowboys turned the last time they hired a head coach.

    Durde was the Cowboys' defensive line coach under Dan Quinn before leaving to be the defensive coordinator under Mike Macdonald in Seattle. He doesn't call the defensive plays for the Seahawks, but he's been part of building one of the NFL's best defenses.

    Rams Assistant HC Kliff Kingsbury.

    Texas Longhorns HC Steve Sarkisian.

    Much like Jones loves connections to the Cowboys, he loves connections to Texas.

    Kingsbury was born and raised in San Antonio. He set records as a high school player in Texas, was inducted into the Texas High School Football Hall of Fame, started at Texas Tech, coached both Houston and Texas Tech to electric offenses and has worked with a lot of high-profile quarterbacks. He wasn't particularly successful as a head coach, but Schottenheimer wasn't particularly successful as an offensive coordinator, and Jones still hired him.

    Industry observers note that sarkisian has been the head coach at UT since 2021. He seemingly generates NFL buzz every offseason. He does have NFL experience as an offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach, but those tenures weren't exactly successful. And his run at Texas has included some high-profile bad losses, including a pair to unranked teams this year. Still, his name will probably come up in NFL circles again.

    Freeman is the hottest college-to-NFL name out there right now. He's been in the mix for other jobs the last two offseasons but decided to stay at Notre Dame, where his team is once again one of the top contenders for the College Football Playoff. He's shown himself to be a good program builder and is the kind of coach who could be a very long-term option if things went well. He'd probably have to be very highly compensated to leave South Bend, though, so it seems pretty unlikely that he'd ever land in Dallas.

    According to recent reports, day's name has also come up in NFL discussions in recent seasons, and with the way Ohio State's season has gone this year (and the way its recruiting class is crumbling), it wouldn't be surprising if this was the offseason where the two sides decided to part ways. Hiring him off his least successful year in college wouldn't be ideal, but that's not really the kind of thing that Jones concerns himself with.

    According to recent reports, joseph got a chance to be a head coach a decade ago, and it didn't go very well. But he's since become a top coordinator again, and maybe he gets another chance at a head-coaching gig. He's not likely to be the hottest name on the market because Sean Payton gets most of the credit for the Broncos' success even though the defense is much better than the offense. However, the Cowboys usually aren't interested in the hottest name on the market because they cost too much to acquire.

    Gannon's tenure as a head coach also didn't go well, but he's been one of the best defensive coordinators in the league this season and was excellent in that role with the Eagles. If Jerry decides fixing the defense is the thing that matters most to him and doesn't want to break the bank, Gannon could be someone he turns to.

    Recent findings suggest that flores is probably the single-best assistant coach in the NFL. His ability to confuse NFL offenses with his schemes is practically unmatched around the league right now. He probably got a raw deal with the Dolphins the first time he was a head coach, and he's annually considered for other jobs. He just always seems to finish as a runner-up, at least in part because he is suing the league for racial discrimination. That's what makes it wildly unlikely that Jones would ever even think about hiring him, let alone actually do it, which is a shame.

    Jaguars DC Anthony Campanile, Jaguars OC Grant Udinski, Ravens OC Declan Doyle, Ravens DC Anthony Weaver, 49ers OC Klay Kubiak, Rams DC Chris Shula, Rams OC Nate Scheelhaase, Patriots TE Coach Thomas Brown, Falcons DC Jeff Ulbrich, Falcons OC Tommy Rees, Steelers DC Patrick Graham, Broncos DC Davis Webb, Vikings QB Coach Josh McCown, Giants DC Dennard Wilson, Jets ST Coach Chris Banjo, Lions OC Drew Petzing, Lions DC Kelvin Sheppard, Panthers OC Brad Idzik, Browns DC Mike Rutenberg, Commanders DC Durante Jones, Bengals OC Dan Pitcher, Texans OC Nick Caley.

    You're likely to see some or all of these names pop up as candidates for whatever jobs open up this coming offseason. The Cowboys choosing from the "up-and-coming assistants" pool seems unlikely given their track record, but it's at least worth noting this group of candidates, since that's where most newly introduced head coaches come from. They have varying levels of worthiness based on what their respective units have done this year and in the past, but they're all going to be on the minds of owners and general managers this hiring season.

    #166259. Tech Report: Arsenal hunger is ominous for rivals as they dismantle Man City

    📅 16 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 30m • 📚 Deep Dive (5940 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Arsenal hunger is ominous for rivals as they dismantle Man City

    📅 16 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 30 min read (5940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~30 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert?
    • Sources indicate that how about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it?
    • Recent findings suggest that so what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert? No. While Ricardo Calafiori’s intervention was dramatic, it wasn’t that. Was it the seamless introduction of the new signings, then? No, it wasn’t that either, despite the excellence of Bruno Guimarães and Christos Tzolis.

    Sources indicate that how about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it? Again, the answer is no. Three unanswered goals against Manchester City will always grab a headline, but scorelines do not always define the nature of a performance or a team’s capabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that so what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably? One word: hunger. The reason this was such an ominous afternoon for the chasing pack is the fact Mikel Arteta’s team played with intensity of a team with everything to prove.

    According to recent reports, title wins can sometimes sate ambition. Players don’t always want to climb the same mountain again, not least if reaching the peak was initially so draining, but everywhere you looked on a day when Cardiff was painted red and white was evidence that Arsenal remain ravenous for success.

    First Guimarães pounced out of the shadows to mug Jérémy Doku, leaving him in a heap. Then there was Gabriel Magalhães thundering into a befuddled Doku, celebrating in front of City’s fans as if he had scored, before Ben White flung himself in front of the Belgian, denying a clear-cut scoring opportunity.

    Ben White to the rescue with an incredible block 🦸📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ZK0cNnFz5N.

    Another notable incident was Martin Odegaard, not long after he had glossed a fabulous display with a third goal, sprinting 30 yards to spook Gianluigi Donnarumma and make the Italian hurry his clearance. The victory was good, the trophy was nice, but the energy heartened Arteta more than anything.

    “They are really good examples,” Arteta stated. “The way the team tracks back is unbelievable, especially when, fitness-wise, we aren’t there yet. We had desire and composure on the ball. When you put your soul and your heart into every action, this is what happens. We want to do it again.

    “The desire comes from them thinking: ‘I want to live that moment again. I want to have all the moments again and I want them to be even bigger.’ We know what it is going to take. We have never done it [retain the Premier League] at this football club. We know it will demand something special.”.

    You could flip that and say it will take something special from the chasers. George Graham and Arsène Wenger could never hold on to the biggest prize during their reigns and you must return to Herbert Chapman, in Arsenal’s thriving 1930s, to find the only manager who went back-to-back.

    It can feel premature (and can be foolish) to go out on a limb before the first weekend, but there was just something about them that felt different. Often in the past they have been overtly tentative when playing City, but they came out of their corner this time swinging – and they landed.

    Enzo Maresca revealed afterwards that he “really didn’t like” how Arsenal had scored their first goal and that was putting it mildly, as there were 10 passes – broken only by the ball bouncing off Elliott Anderson’s shins – before Myles Lewis-Skelly ushered Calafiori into wreak havoc.

    You had to go back to 1968, when City played West Brom, to find the last first-minute goal – City’s Bobby Owen was the scorer that day – and how Calafiori enjoyed it, shaking his fist in delight as Arsenal’s noisy fans reminded everyone of their status.

    Riccardo Calafiori gives Arsenal the lead after just 24 seconds 🤯The assist from Myles Lewis-Skelly 👏📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/aU0UsCB1Xs.

    It has been revealed that here was a rude awakening for Anderson, City’s new £116m man. He was ever so slightly off the pace and that allowed Lewis-Skelly to slip a beautiful ball in behind the FA Cup winners’ defence and invite Calafiori to do the rest, which he did with assurance.

    Sources indicate that when Maresca watches back the video, he will see Abdukodir Khusanov sleeping and Phil Foden failing to press, but that should not detract from the quality of Arsenal’s interchanging – and it should also make whoever is hawking Lewis-Skelly around to clubs to think again. Why would he leave this?

    It has been revealed that it should not have been the case that a goal so soon should have governed how the game progressed, but that is exactly what happened as Arsenal completely dominated. Whenever they lost possession, they recovered it as a matter of urgency. Without Pep Guardiola on the touchline, City were like Samson after Delilah shaved his hair, devoid of all power.

    City, in contrast to their opponents, revealed a complete lack of desire and the second goal arrived when Odegaard was allowed time to flip a ball to the back post, where upcoming boy Tzolis was arriving. The Greek headed back into the six-yard area and Kai Havertz did the rest.

    Kai Havertz finishes off a well-worked move to double Arsenal's lead 🤩📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/tGkxCIBV8F.

    Arsenal were criticised – fairly – during their title-winning campaign for being too physical and relying on gamesmanship, but if Havertz and Odegaard can stay fit for a prolonged period, the difference in style will be like night and day.

    Throw in Tzolis, who was tricky and dynamic in Cardiff, to the mix and there will be another enhancement. He looks considerably better than Gabriel Martinelli, with more end product, and Bukayo Saka will do more down the right than Noni Madueke, who started here.

    Maresca knew, with his team lacking fitness, that it would be difficult to overhaul the deficit once they had gone two goals behind but, really, he was lucky that Arsenal did not administer a genuine hiding which, at one stage, seemed as though they might.

    Goal number three arrived just after the interval, again Lewis-Skelly and Tzolis were involved, combining to enable Odegaard to waltz into the area, hoodwinking Donnarumma so he sat down before sliding a contemptuous finish beyond him.

    Now it is Arsenal and Mikel Arteta who have a league title behind them, while Enzo Maresca is the manager hoping to build credibility as City turn the page post-Pep Guardiola.

Christos Tzolis in and Leandro Trossard out looks canny business, but falls into the category of like for like.

    Although Arsenal held their nerve to see off City in the title race, they failed to win in three attempts against their rivals, including a limp defeat in the Carabao Cup final at Wembley. Arsenal also failed to win, or score, against Liverpool in the Premier League last season so their record in the substantial games is an area for improvement.

    Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH

    📅 28 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • Recent findings suggest that on Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off.
    • It has been revealed that bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Recent findings suggest that on Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off. Nottingham, unbeaten in their last nine matches, has impressed this season with outstanding defensive work. Bournemouth, coached by Andoni Iraola and now unbeaten in 12 games, takes a completely different tactical approach compared to most other teams. In an interview with TNT Sports, Guardiola remarked: “Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton, and Liverpool play.” What exactly are these teams doing differently? Bournemouth’s approach will be analyzed in detail based on this match.

    It has been revealed that bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao. Bielsa, widely known in the Premier League as the coach who led Leeds United to promotion, gained recognition for his style of play characterized by exceptionally high intensity in all phases of the game. According to Iraola, his own footballing philosophy has been significantly shaped by his former coach Bielsa.

    In an interview with Sky, back when he was still managing Rayo Vallecano, Iraola stated: “I was very lucky to play for him (Bielsa) for two seasons as a player. I think he has another vision of football. They were two very good seasons for us, and, for me, it was a different knowledge.” He also explained: “I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him. I use a lot of things, especially with the ball. Offensively, his teams are very dynamic. He is willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder, offensively.”.

    Iraola’s tactical concept can be described as “organized chaos.” The aim is not to implement a positional system with perfect patterns of play. Instead, the focus is on creating problems for opposing teams by generating chaos. The idea is to force the opponent into unfamiliar, uncontrolled phases of play. A particularly important concept within this is highly intense, man-oriented, hybrid attacking pressing, designed to force the opponent into quick turnovers and a fast-paced, direct game.

    „It is true that we like, and we perform better, in high-tempo games. We need to run a lot. We don’t need so much control, not in every single play, but I think we have the legs, we have the willingness, to go up and down.“ – Iraola.

    According to recent reports, accordingly, Iraola’s style of play could face challenges against deep-lying teams that deliberately thrive on minimal possession. These teams don’t need to engage with Bournemouth’s high-intensity game but can instead remain compact out of possession. They are not required to build up play from the back under Bournemouth’s pressing to maintain controlled possession but can focus on their own offensive transitions. This season, Nottingham has been one of the most successful teams in executing such an approach. Consequently, it was particularly intriguing to observe how Iraola’s Bournemouth would operate in possession against Nottingham’s deep block.

    Iraola describes his philosophy in possession as follows:.

    “We have to prepare [positional] patterns, but we cannot just prioritise them. If you can see that you don’t have a teammate ahead, forget about the pattern, just drive the ball and try to force things to happen. I want him to attack first.”.

    Here lies the challenge I encountered while analyzing the game against Nottingham: how do you describe intentionally provoked chaos, where there are barely any fixed patterns? Only a few predefined sequences can be identified within the positional framework. The crucial question, therefore, is: what reference points structure Bournemouth’s possession play, and which principles of play create this chaos? Or, put simply: what “tools” does Iraola use in his style of play? To answer this, the positional framework of the game against Nottingham will first be examined.

    Industry observers note that starting from a nominal 4-2-3-1 formation, Nottingham defended out of possession in a 4-4-1-1 or 4-5-1 structure. Nottingham focused primarily on defending and largely conceded possession to Bournemouth, a characteristic approach for the team. Under coach Simoes Espirito Santo, Nottingham has averaged just 40% possession this season.

    Sources indicate that bournemouth, meanwhile, operated in possession with a positional 2-4-4 or 2-3-2-3 structure, featuring wide wingers and full-backs. From this setup, Bournemouth attempted to break through Nottingham’s deep block. On the (left) No. 10 position, Kluivert stood out with his exceptional dribbling ability and high agility. Central midfielder Christie alternated between the deeper right half-space as a right-sided No. 10 and the No. 6 position.

    It has been revealed that nottingham was often forced back into their own half from an initially higher defensive pressing. When Nottingham attempted to press higher, Bournemouth’s center-backs positioned themselves wide, and goalkeeper Kepa moved up to form part of the back line. This made it nearly impossible for Nottingham’s lone striker to put significant pressure on the ball carrier. As a result, Nottingham dropped deep, retreated, and refrained from pressing the ball-carrying center-backs.

    „I sometimes value much more a player carrying the ball and forcing things to happen. I think when you play too positional – one, two touches to find a free man – you sometimes lose the initiative from the players to just take their man on and attack the spaces.” – Iraola.

    This approach meant that Bournemouth’s center-backs were frequently required to dribble forward against stationary opponents, forcing defenders to commit. This often created 5v4 or 4v4 situations on the flanks, caused by the strong lateral movements of striker Ouattara and attacking midfielder Kluivert, combined with the forward dribbling of the center-backs. When no passingoptions were available, the team didn’t rebuild play, as is typical for positionally oriented teams. Instead, Bournemouth’s left center-back, Huijsen, was occasionally seen dribbling directly at the opponent’s last defensive line. It can be concluded that one of Iraola’s key principles of play is to attack vertically with the ball as early as possible.

    Center-back Huijsen dribbles toward the final defensive line himself due to a lack of better-positioned deeper passing options.

    The situations on the flanks during the center-back’s dribbling were played out in various ways. Sometimes the ball was passed to the wide player on the wing, who was tasked with taking on a 1v1 duel. This player was consistently supported by the full-back in a dual-width setup.

    In a recent development, particularly noteworthy were the positional rotations of the 3-4 players on the flanks. Full-backs, attacking midfielder Kluivert, striker Ouattara, and the winger frequently rotated out of their positions, occupying different spaces. What stood out was the consistent presence of a dynamic deep run within these rotations, forcing the opponent to cover the run and thereby creating space between their players.

    The positional rotations with deep runs create passing options.

    It has been revealed that for example, the left-back Kerkez, during the center-back’s dribble, occasionally made deep runs into the half-space. Similarly, attacking midfielder Kluivert was often involved, sometimes shifting laterally to receive the ball and then driving forward at pace to attack the defensive block.

    According to recent reports, nottingham responded to this from the 30th minute by attempting to apply more pressure on Bournemouth’s ball-carrying center-backs. The 4-4-1-1 shape was adjusted by removing the man-marking on defensive midfielder Adams. Instead, Nottingham transitioned into a 4-4-2 setup, aiming to position Adams in the cover shadow and step out earlier to press the center-backs. However, Bournemouth’s goalkeeper Kepa played so high in the back line that he was still able to connect with the now even wider-positioned center-backs, allowing them to continue dribbling forward.

    The goalkeeper stepping into the back line creates a 4v2 situation, allowing the center-backs to dribble forward with less pressure from opponents.

    “I would say they have the freedom to risk a little bit in the dribbles.“ – Iraola.

    Another key principle of Bournemouth’s possession game is diagonal, vertical dribbling. These serve as a chaos factor and are constantly utilized across all positions. As long as no teammate is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal, players are given the freedom to dribble. The skillful dribblers on the wings, the striker, and attacking midfielder Kluivert fit perfectly into this principle. The spaces opened up through the aforementioned rotations, particularly between the opposing players on the flanks, were mostly attacked through dribbling rather than passing.

    The core idea behind this focus on dribbling is closely aligned with the concept of relationism. The goal is to make the team’s decisions less predictable for the opponent and to create a certain degree of chaos. Traditional positional play often limits players’ individual freedom, which reduces the element of surprise. However, Iraola’s execution of possession football differs significantly from relationism.

    Instead of using a tighter structure to encourage combinations between players, rotations and larger distances between players are used to create spaces intended to be attacked through dribbling. It is crucial that these dribbles are always executed as vertical actions, continually putting the opponent under defensive pressure and thereby opening up other options.

    Recent findings suggest that due to the larger spaces on the flanks, many dribbles are initiated on the wing, supported by the dual-width occupation of the winger and full-back. To enforce a successful follow-up action against deep-lying opponents, proper box occupation is a fundamental requirement. Iraola’s teams often flood the opponent’s penalty area with up to seven players, forcing the opposition right in front of their own goal. The goal is not necessarily to find the open player but to increase the likelihood of winning the ball after a cross in the penalty area. Second balls also play a significant role in this approach.

    Risky dribbles have the additional advantage of provoking more frequent transition moments. When the opponent tries to transition offensively, they lose their compact defensive shape. Bournemouth’s flexible rest defense allows the ball to be immediately recovered after a loss of possession. Bournemouth’s rest defense typically consists of 3-4 players, depending on the attacking structure. In addition to the two center-backs, defensive midfielder Adams and the inverted, far-side full-back provide cover. If both full-backs or Adams are involved in the attack, Christie drops deeper to provide support and shifts closer to the ball.

    Industry observers note that on one hand, it’s notable to highlight the excellent sense of positioning from the two central midfielders, Adams and Christie, in anticipating potential turnovers. Their ability to read these moments and their spatial awareness lead to many successful counter-pressing actions. On the other hand, the immediate pressure applied to the ball-carrying opponent after a turnover is notable, leaving the opposition with little opportunity to create controlled possession phases.

    Sources indicate that as a result, Nottingham’s offensive presence in the first half was minimal. Successful offensive transitions by Simoes Espirito Santo’s team were extremely rare.

    Industry observers note that the rest-defense structure in the 21st minute consists of the inverted Kerkez, the shifting defensive midfielder Adams, and the center-backs. At the same time, the ball-near teammates position themselves in response to the dribble in a way that allows them to immediately apply pressure if needed.

    In a recent development, another key principle of Bournemouth’s play is that after regaining possession, the first action is immediately directed forward. In contrast to traditionally positional teams, control is not sought through possession in chaotic situations but rather through constant transitions. The goal is to prevent the opponent from regaining their structure and settling into their usual rhythm. This creates intense pressure for Bournemouth’s opponents. As a result, Bournemouth often didn’t even need to break down Nottingham’s defensive block because the opponent never had the chance to regain their typical structure.

    Recent findings suggest that after recovering the ball, Bournemouth consistently looked to play forward into pressure. When positioned deeper (closer to their own goal), players in the forward zones immediately made runs into space to create vertical passing options. Even if the Bournemouth player who regained the ball was immediately under pressure, the first action was directed forward.

    In a recent development, if necessary, a long ball was played toward the opponent’s defensive line, with a focus on winning second balls. This pressing game with an emphasis on second balls—often referred to as “kick and rush”—generated additional forced transition situations, preventing the opponent from finding their usual shape. The fact that four of Bournemouth’s five goals against the typically deep-lying Nottingham team came from deliberately provoked transition moments highlights the effectiveness of this approach.

    Industry observers note that in the second half, Nottingham switched to an attacking press in an attempt to create more scoring opportunities and overturn the 1-0 deficit. However, Nottingham was unable to pin Bournemouth in their own half as planned. Instead, Bournemouth played targeted long balls to one of their four advanced attackers or to the half-high positioned full-backs. Through a combination of winning second balls, dribbles, and central midfielders following up for lay-offs, Bournemouth was able to quickly progress into space and control the game from their own half. This led to Bournemouth scoring their second and third goals in quick succession. The final result was a resounding 5-0 victory for Iraola’s side.

    So, what exactly causes the chaos in Bournemouth’s possession play? In summary, it is a combination of the principles discussed: playing vertically as early as possible; dribbling diagonally and vertically as long as no player is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal; and making the first action after regaining possession a forward one. The focus on vertical zones (reference point: opponent players) and second balls (reference point: the opponent’s goal) creates an intense and dynamic style of play that prevents the opponent from settling into their usual structure. Bournemouth is further aided by their attacking press, which was not analyzed in detail in this article but consistently provokes additional transition situations.

    What can other teams take away from Bournemouth’s possession approach without abandoning their own philosophy? One lesson is the courage to consistently seek depth, provided the team has appropriate counter-pressing structures in place. Additionally, the dynamism of individual actions at Bournemouth is remarkable. Rarely have I seen such explosive runs into depth from other teams.

    The final question is: what do the teams mentioned by Guardiola in the aforementioned interview have in common? All of them attack the depth swiftly and frequently, making the game incredibly dynamic and intense. This forces the opponent to make decisions faster. After all, the main difference between good and very good players is the time it takes to make a good decision.

    According to recent reports, my recommendation is to watch games from 30 years ago. It swiftly becomes apparent that football has become faster and more demanding.

    Sources indicate that “For me, the players are better than in 2003. They have to do the same things, but much faster. The physical demands are ridiculous. I doubt I could have played at this rhythm.” – Iraola.

    Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally crucial to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a newly introduced collective bargaining agreement.

    Recent findings suggest that the collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

    The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

    The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

    Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a latest CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

    To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a fresh CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

    The owners of Major League Baseball have launched legal action against the MLBPA, reports the Wall Street Journal. The lawsuit is a preemptive shot by the league, asking the court to declare that the forthcoming lockout is legal "under antitrust law and cannot be enjoined by a court -- even if the players give up their union status, as the league anticipates they will.".

    The lawsuit names eight defendants, the members of the MLBPA's executive subcommittee: Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Chris Bassitt, Marcus Semien, Jake Cronenworth, Brent Suter, Pete Fairbanks and Cedric Mullins.

    "MLB believes that the MLBPA is planning to 'disclaim' its status as the players' bargaining representative and then argue that the lockout constitutes an illegal group boycott. Players would then theoretically have standing to sue the league on antitrust grounds, exposing MLB to the possibility of having to pay treble damages, or three times the players' proven losses.".

    The MLBPA has replied (via The Athletic):.

    "The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous. We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.".

    Industry observers note that in earlier iterations of negotiations, MLB proposed a salary-escrow system like the ones found in the NBA and NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld in case league revenue projections fall short for a given year. If that's the case, then that money in escrow goes back to the league to cover the revenue shortfalls. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA has pointedly opposed the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries. In its latest statement on the negotiations, MLB withdrew the escrow proposal. "For months, union leadership has attacked the escrow provision used in other sports and mischaracterized the glitch as the end of guaranteed contracts," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin noted in a statement. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal, removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the new salary cap and floor system.".

    The specifics of the newly introduced proposal, which like all other league proposals thus far been tied to the players' accceptance of a cap and floor on team payrolls:.

    In response, interim union head Bruce Meyer released the following statement:.

    Industry observers note that "MLB today modified its salary cap proposal to 'eliminate' escrow, but once again it provides no real benefit under their proposed cap system. Instead of holding back player money each year, MLB's fresh proposal is to take that same amount of money out of players' pockets in the following year. It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap - to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement. This is yet another example of how MLB's salary cap proposal pits player against player, past, present, and future.".

    In a recent development, in their latest bargaining session, the MLBPA maintained its previous proposals aimed to increase revenue sharing support for small market teams, including a mechanism designed to punish teams that do not put revenue sharing funds into the roster. The union also said the proposal is designed to remove "any league excuses for the continuation of blackouts.".

    Here are the details of the union's latest proposal:.

    As for MLB's proposal, it now includes a $1 million minimum salary (previous proposals were described as $1 million but not quite that amount), and a new series of bonuses for all player classes:.

    Did Chiefs get hosed by NFL clock controversy? Breaking down the final seconds of Bills' wild Thanksgiving win

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the NFL gave us a wild day of football on Thanksgiving, and the action didn't end until late Thursday night when the Bills' kicker Tyler Bass hit a 57-yard field goal on the final play to beat the Chiefs 13-10.
    • It has been revealed that after a punt by Buffalo, the Chiefs had a first-and-10 from their own 11-yard line with just 26 seconds left to play.
    • On first down, Patrick Mahomes fumbled the shotgun snap, and that's where things started to get interesting with the clock.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the NFL gave us a wild day of football on Thanksgiving, and the action didn't end until late Thursday night when the Bills' kicker Tyler Bass hit a 57-yard field goal on the final play to beat the Chiefs 13-10. Although the Bills got the win, it appears they may have gotten some help from the clock operator, who might have given Buffalo a few extra seconds at the end of the game.

    Let's break down exactly what happened.

    It has been revealed that after a punt by Buffalo, the Chiefs had a first-and-10 from their own 11-yard line with just 26 seconds left to play. The Chiefs couldn't simply kneel the ball and take the game to overtime because the Bills had all three timeouts, so Kansas City had to try to put together a drive.

    On first down, Patrick Mahomes fumbled the shotgun snap, and that's where things started to get interesting with the clock.

    After Mahomes fell on the ball, the Bills called a timeout, and the clock stopped at 19 seconds. However, before the Chiefs ran their next play, six seconds were added to the game clock, bringing it to 25 seconds. This means that the first-down play only took one second.

    I am at a loss for words as how this first play only took *one* second off the game clock.Chiefs could have handled the ensuing sequence and punt differently and Buffalo potentially does not end up with enough time for the field goal attempt. pic.twitter.com/ILkv8LEXR7.

    Industry observers note that the clip above was shared by Super Bowl-winning analytics consultant Ryan Paganetti, who used to make a living helping teams handle late-game situations like this. He was one of many people who were stunned that only one second came off the clock.

    On the play, the whistle blew with 24 seconds left, and if you factor in that Bills head coach Joe Brady had to call a timeout, it seems like at least three seconds should have run off the clock.

    On the next play, Emmett Johnson ran for a five-yard gain on second down. This play started with 25 seconds left on the clock and ended when the refs blew the whistle at 19 seconds. However, the officials added one more second to the clock, moving it to 20 before the start of the next play.

    On third down, Mahomes threw an incompletion to Travis Kelce, which left just 15 seconds to play. At that point, it was total chaos: The Chiefs had to punt, and the Bills tipped the punt, making it more returnable for Greg Dortch, who took it 17 yards to Kansas City's 39-yard line. Dortch was tackled with four seconds left, which was just enough time for Bass to hit his game-winning field goal.

    Industry observers note that this final sequence is pure cinema. pic.twitter.com/jO4Fd8IOgu.

    The Bills definitely seemed to benefit from extra time here, but it's hard to say exactly how much. By my count, they got an extra three seconds, and in that case, Bass still would have been able to attempt the game-winning field goal with one second left. Other NFL reporters thought the Bills got even more time, with some believing Buffalo got anywhere from four to seven extra seconds.

    According to recent reports, if the Bills did get four to seven extra seconds, that would have created an interesting situation to end regulation. Matt Araiza's final punt would have come with just eight to 11 seconds left instead of 15. In that situation, instead of returning the kick, Dortch could have called for a fair catch, and that would have set up a possible fair-catch free kick to win the game (this can be attempted even if the clock hits zero seconds on the play). The Chiefs also could have punted it out of bounds, or they could have had Araiza hit it low to ensure the ball would bounce so there would be no fair catch, but in either of those situations, the clock likely wouldn't have run out, and Buffalo still would have had time for one more play.

    Sources indicate that in the end, it does seem like the Bills got the benefit of a few extra seconds, but it's impossible to say whether that cost the Chiefs the game. Kansas City also had another controversy in the fourth quarter, when Rashee Rice made a catch for a first down on third-and-10 that was eventually overturned. Rice states he caught the ball, but the officials felt otherwise.

    Although some NFL fans seem to think the Chiefs get every call, this game proves that not everything goes their way.

    #166251. Broncos at Steelers: Why the NFL isn't allowed to schedule the Black Friday game for primetime

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (374 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Broncos at Steelers: Why the NFL isn't allowed to schedule the Black Friday game for primetime

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that for the fourth straight year, the NFL is holding a Black Friday game, and for the fourth straight year, it will kick off at 3 p.m.
    • With the Broncos and Steelers heading into a huge matchup, the NFL would probably prefer to put the Black Friday game in primetime — especially with all the Aaron Rodgers' drama surrounding the game — but the league can't do that thanks to a 65-year-old law.
    • It has been revealed that under the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, the league isn't allowed to televise any games on Friday or Saturday from the second weekend in September through the second weekend in December.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that for the fourth straight year, the NFL is holding a Black Friday game, and for the fourth straight year, it will kick off at 3 p.m. ET, which makes it the most bizarre game on the NFL schedule. It's the only regular-season game all year that kicks off at 3 p.m.

    With the Broncos and Steelers heading into a huge matchup, the NFL would probably prefer to put the Black Friday game in primetime — especially with all the Aaron Rodgers' drama surrounding the game — but the league can't do that thanks to a 65-year-old law.

    It has been revealed that under the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, the league isn't allowed to televise any games on Friday or Saturday from the second weekend in September through the second weekend in December. Instead, those two days have been earmarked for high school and college football. However, there is a loophole in this rule: the NFL is ALLOWED to schedule a Friday game as long as it ends before 6 p.m. local time, which is how the league settled on a 3 p.m. ET kickoff time. It's basically the latest the game could start without running afoul of the SBA.

    The NFL has generally avoided this issue by just not scheduling any Friday games. Since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, the league has only played a total of 16 Friday games and six of those have essentially been holiday games that were either played on Christmas Eve, Christmas or New Year's Eve. Those three holidays come AFTER the second weekend in December, so the NFL is allowed to put those games in primetime. For Black Friday, the game has to be in the afternoon.

    The Black Friday game has worked out so well for the NFL that the league is actually kicking around the idea of adding a second game to the day. If that happened, it would likely be a doubleheader, with the first game kicking off at 12 p.m. ET and the second at 3 p.m. ET. Roger Goodell floated the doubleheader idea earlier this year, and although it didn't happen, it could still certainly be something we see on the schedule next year.

    • Recent findings suggest that inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place.
    • It has been revealed that inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Recent findings suggest that inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

    It has been revealed that inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

    Sources indicate that inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

    As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

    Industry observers note that to build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

    Industry observers note that the primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

    Recent findings suggest that if only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be swiftly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

    It has been revealed that to effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

    Sources indicate that through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

    Even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

    This three-man buildup creates upcoming passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

    According to recent reports, due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

    According to recent reports, additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

    Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

    Sources indicate that the follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

    Sources indicate that one of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

    According to recent reports, while striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

    It has been revealed that the pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

    Industry observers note that A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

    It has been revealed that another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

    Recent findings suggest that depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

    Industry observers note that once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

    While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

    Especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

    Industry observers note that as the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

    It has been revealed that inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

    It has been revealed that in possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

    Breaking: Connor Bedard injury: Blackhawks star's latest concern shines light on a stalled out rebuild in Chicago

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An awful start for the Chicago Blackhawks only got worse on Monday night when the team announced that captain and superstar forward Connor Bedard would miss four months after undergoing right shoulder surgery.
    • Industry observers note that on Nov.
    • Industry observers note that bedard missed the first two weeks of the season while recovering from surgery on his left shoulder in the offseason.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An awful start for the Chicago Blackhawks only got worse on Monday night when the team announced that captain and superstar forward Connor Bedard would miss four months after undergoing right shoulder surgery.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 17, Bedard injured his shoulder on a face-off and left the ice in a lot of discomfort. After deliberating whether to rehab the shoulder or get surgery to repair the glitch, Bedard opted for the latter half. That will sideline him longer now, but it could provide a more permanent fix.

    Industry observers note that bedard missed the first two weeks of the season while recovering from surgery on his left shoulder in the offseason. The Blackhawks captain suffered that injury during summer training -- and that also occurred on a seemingly innocuous play.

    Even after Bedard's initial injury, Chicago hoped that the 2026-27 season would be a step in the right direction amid a lengthy rebuild. Instead, the team is on track to finish with fewer points this year than last year -- despite playing two more games.

    Industry observers note that the Blackhawks are 8-14-2, which is good for 30th place in the NHL. Only the aging Pittsburgh Penguins and actively tanking Vancouver Canucks sit below them. The prospects Chicago has drafted in recent years haven't shown adequate process at the NHL level, and they've got no veteran support around them.

    With Bedard out for an extended period of time, the Blackhawks must re-assess their long-term vision.

    When healthy, Bedard has shown that he can be a true superstar. The 21-year-old has 82 goals and 139 assists in 234 career games, and he began the 2025-26 season on a torrid pace before, well, suffering a shoulder injury.

    And therein lies the biggest question about Bedard's future as a true force in the NHL. Is this just bad luck, or will his lack of durability prevent him from reaching the potential that's evident when the puck is on his stick? Chicago can only hope its the former, but this isn't the first time Bedard has missed significant time due to injury.

    Industry observers note that this is now Bedard's fourth NHL season, and he's played 70-plus games just once. That was in the 2024-25 season, when he played all 82 games and tallied 67 points.

    According to recent reports, last season, a right shoulder injury forced him to miss 13 games and snuffed out his tremendous start. Months later, Bedard injured his left shoulder after taking a spill during summer workouts. That prompted one surgery, and his latest right shoulder injury prompted another procedure less than five months later.

    I'm certainly not a doctor, but two shoulder surgeries that close together seems concerning, especially for how much the Blackhawks have invested in Bedard.

    Sources indicate that in 2022-23, the franchise completely demolished its roster in hopes of landing the No. 1 overall pick. It worked, and Chicago got to draft Bedard, the consensus top prospect in the class. This past summer, Bedard and the Hawks agreed to a five-year contract extension worth $75 million.

    If Bedard gets healthy and plays anywhere near his peak, that will be a discount. If injuries continue to limit him, the Blackhawks will have a serious problem on their hands, but that probably goes without saying.

    Even with Bedard in the mix, the Blackhawks' rebuild wasn't going particularly well. Chicago hasn't finished above .500 since the 2019-20 season, which was cut short due to the COVID-19 pandemic and was three years before they selected Bedard in the 2023 NHL Draft.

    Sources indicate that the upshot of all that stinking is that the Hawks stocked up on premium draft capital. With that, they've built what should and exciting young core for the franchise. Not including Bedard, Chicago has seven skaters who were selected in the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

    Kantserov has shown scoring touch at the NHL level, Nazar has been inconsistent and flashed upside and Rinzel has started to show signs of progress on the back end. Other than that, none of those young guns are ready for primetime. That's not say they will never get there. In particular, Frondell and Levshunov have the tools to get there.

    In a recent development, it's just that the results have been really ugly to this point. According to Natural Stat Trick, the Blackhawks rank 30th in expected goals share at 42.5%. The team's minus-32 goal differential ranks 31st in the NHL. To put it more succintly, Chicago is getting what it deserves more often than not.

    In a recent development, with Bedard out for the next four months, it's time to see who can sink and who can swim. Stop playing 37-year-old Ian Cole almost 20 minutes per game and let defensive prospects see the ice more. Tyler Bertuzzi has been incredibly ineffective, and his contract is moveable. Trade him to a contender and open up another spot for a young player in the top six.

    If the team doesn't make any progress over the last 60 games of the season, it may be time for a wholesale changes at the top. General manager Kyle Davidson was tasked with orchestrating a rebuild that's going nowhere rapidly. Jeff Blashill is 37-53-16 behind the Blackhawks' bench, and he's 241-314-88 in his coaching career.

    In a recent development, if Chicago continues to flail at the bottom of the standings, how much worse could it possibly get? A fresh set of eyes in the front office and a new voice in the locker room wouldn't be the worst ideas.

    #166248. MLB rumors: Kevin Gausman finds fresh home, plus latest on Royals, Phillies, Rockies, Cubs, Mariners, more

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)
