    Mason Rudolph and Steelers defense can clean up Aaron Rodgers' mess, but the franchise's problems run deeper

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, days after Aaron Rodgers set fire to the place on his way out of town, the Steelers turned to the same quarterback who rescued their season three years ago.
    • Is this a dead-cat-bounce win for a team that just endured Aaron Rodgers Armageddon, or is there something here?
    • Recent findings suggest that and after all that's happened, the Steelers are somehow 7-4.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Well, of course Mason Rudolph was the answer.

    In a recent development, days after Aaron Rodgers set fire to the place on his way out of town, the Steelers turned to the same quarterback who rescued their season three years ago. And against a Broncos team that came to Pittsburgh with eight wins and legitimate Super Bowl aspirations, the Steelers were unequivocally the better football team.

    So now what? Is this a dead-cat-bounce win for a team that just endured Aaron Rodgers Armageddon, or is there something here? And if the Broncos can entertain thoughts of winning a Super Bowl with what they've gotten out of Bo Nix this season, why can't the Steelers make something of their remaining season with Rudolph?

    Recent findings suggest that and after all that's happened, the Steelers are somehow 7-4. If you squint, there are reasons to believe they can make something of this season. There are also reasons, if you're clear-headed and rational, to be concerned about what another nine- or 10-win season might mean for an organization that has spent years mistaking winning for progress.

    Maybe the Steelers found a way to salvage a season that, 48 hours ago, felt unsalvageable. What they can't afford to do is mistake that for having figured out their future.

    According to recent reports, we've previously written about the Broncos, whose ability to win close games has been unprecedented. They've done it despite routinely getting outgained and despite uneven play from Nix.

    In a recent development, but here's the thing: Coming into their Black Friday matchup, the Steelers had played better defense than the Broncos, hadn't been outgained by anything close to 700 yards and hadn't needed nearly as many late-game heroics to win. The Broncos had two more victories to show for it, but there wasn't nearly as much separating these teams as their records might suggest.

    Steelers vs. Broncos entering Week 12.

    Industry observers note that nix had been playing considerably better of late. After an underwhelming first six games, he was averaging 52 more passing yards per game and had thrown six touchdowns against two interceptions over his next four starts. Denver won all four games, scoring at least 26 points each time.

    Friday served as a reminder of just how much Denver needs Nix to take care of the football. One of his greatest strengths coming into the season was his ability to avoid sacks, which helped offset his inability to consistently generate substantial plays. The Steelers defense turned a Nix sack-fumble and a pick-six into 14 points in the first half alone. When it was over, Patrick Graham's group had sacked Nix twice and held him to 169 passing yards with no touchdowns and two interceptions.

    According to recent reports, pittsburgh has a defense capable of doing that to opposing QBs. The question, as it has been for the better part of eight seasons, is whether the Steelers' own quarterback situation can overcome replacement-level play.

    It has been revealed that nobody's confusing Rudolph with anything more than a reliable journeyman backup. They need him to be better than Aaron Rodgers, which, despite everything Rodgers accomplished in his first two decades in the league, was immediately obvious on Friday.

    And it's worth remembering what Rudolph did the last time the Steelers found themselves in such a predicament. In his three regular-season starts in 2023, he averaged more than 10 yards per attempt, threw three touchdowns without an interception and won all three games. Nobody benefited more from Rudolph's willingness to push the ball downfield than George Pickens.

    Rudolph, career entering Friday.

    Reprising the role of Pickens on Friday: DK Metcalf!

    On Friday, Rudolph completed 9 of 15 passes for 142 yards, including a 58-yarder to rookie Germie Bernard, a 37-yarder to Roman Wilson and a 22-yard touchdown to the aforementioned Mr. Metcalf. Given what the Steelers have invested in their wide receivers and how little they've gotten in return, it'll be worth watching whether Rudolph can consistently get more out of that group than Rodgers did.

    Recent findings suggest that if Rudolph can do for the Steelers what he did back in '23, it's reasonable to think that, yes, this group will make the playoffs – and, yes, will be underdogs to actually win a playoff game. The bigger concern, however, is how the organization might interpret that success given the last decade.

    Because we've been here before. Three years ago, the Steelers were 6-4, had set the forward-passing game back decades, and eventually turned to Mason Rudolph to save their season. Since then, they've changed coordinators and head coaches, completely overhauled their quarterback room (twice), and committed $209 million to two of the NFL's least productive wide receivers (whether due to injury or inconsistency).

    Sources indicate that and what do they have to show for it? Consider this: Of the 133 NFL teams to start 6-4 since 2000, only three were less efficient throwing the football than the '26 Steelers: the 2000 Lions, the 2022 Jets and … the aforementioned 2023 Steelers (as measured by EPA per dropback).

    Expand that group to include seven previous teams that started 6-4 and also really struggled to throw the ball, and here's what happened: Not a single, solitary one of them improved its record the following season. In fact, together they won just 35% of their games, and four of those seven lost at least 12 times.

    In a recent development, and what did those franchises do in the seasons that followed? Some found their way out of the dysfunction; others made decisions that would haunt them for years—and, in some cases, decades.

    6-4 teams with struggling passing offenses, 2000-25.

    Teams since 2000 that started 6-4 with an EPA/dropback of -0.07 or worse.

    In 2003, four years removed from Dan Marino's retirement, Miami had Ricky Williams in the backfield and a defense that featured Jason Taylor, Zach Thomas, Junior Seau, Patrick Surtain and Sam Madison. Dave Wannstedt's team won 10 games with Jay Fiedler and Brian Griese at quarterback. The Dolphins missed the playoffs, but it's not difficult to understand why they might have thought they were a quarterback away.

    They traded a future second-round pick for AJ Feeley, who threw 15 interceptions in eight starts in 2004. Williams abruptly retired, Wannstedt resigned and the Dolphins won four games. Enter Nick Saban, who got them back to 9-7 in his first season with Gus Frerotte.

    And then came perhaps the most consequential personnel decision of the century for the Dolphins: In March 2006, Miami passed on Drew Brees, who was coming off shoulder surgery, and traded a second-round pick for Daunte Culpepper, who was recovering from a serious knee injury.

    Recent findings suggest that saban has since noted he wanted Brees, but the Dolphins' doctors wouldn't clear him. Either way, Culpepper started four games for Miami, Brees spent the next 15 seasons in Fresh Orleans, and Saban was in Tuscaloosa less than a year later. The Dolphins went 1-15 in 2007.

    Then there's Detroit, which replaced longtime executive Chuck Schmidt with Matt Millen following its nine-win season in 2000. Millen hired Marty Mornhinweg; the Lions won two games, and a year later they drafted Joey Harrington with the third overall pick. Detroit drafted a wide receiver in the first round in each of the next three years: Charles Rogers, Roy Williams and Mike Williams.

    The Lions went 31-97 from 2001-2008, including a 0-16 finish in Millen's final season.

    Recent findings suggest that they finally got it right at quarterback, drafting Matthew Stafford first overall in 2009, but went 74-90-1 in his starts over 12 seasons and never won a playoff game. Stafford won a Super Bowl in his first season after Detroit traded him to the Rams in 2021, and the Lions finally figured it out after hiring GM Brad Holmes and head coach Dan Campbell. With Jared Goff, Detroit went from three wins in 2021 to nine in 2022 to 12 and an NFC Championship game appearance in 2023. Detroit won more playoff games that season (two) than it had in the previous 65 seasons combined (one).

    Industry observers note that the 2022 Jets had the NFL's fourth-ranked scoring defense, both the Offensive and Defensive Rookies of the Year in Garrett Wilson and Sauce Gardner … and a problem at quarterback. Former No. 2 overall pick Zach Wilson didn't come close to living up to his draft status, and Robert Saleh's team went 1-6 down the stretch.

    General manager Joe Douglas traded for Rodgers, the Jets hired Nathaniel Hackett as offensive coordinator and brought in some of Rodgers' former teammates. Rodgers tore his Achilles in the opener, New York won seven games – just as they had the season before – and they doubled down the following offseason, eventually trading for Davante Adams.

    The Jets did improve throwing the football in 2024. The defense, meanwhile, went from one of the league's best to a liability. They won five games, fired Saleh and Douglas, moved on from Rodgers and won three games in 2025.

    This should sound familiar. One difference: Gardner, Wilson, Quinnen Williams and Breece Hall were all 25 or younger when New York first decided they were just a QB away. Pittsburgh doesn't have that luxury with T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey.

    According to recent reports, bill O'Brien's Texans won exactly nine games in each of his first three seasons as head coach. Houston gave Brock Osweiler $72 million in 2016; he threw more interceptions than touchdowns, and general manager Rick Smith spent the following offseason getting himself out of the mess.

    According to recent reports, the Texans attached a second-round pick to Osweiler to get Cleveland to take his contract, then gave the Browns two first-rounders to move from No. 25 to No. 12 to draft Deshaun Watson. Watson tore his ACL as a rookie, but Houston won 21 games and two division titles over the next two seasons.

    It has been revealed that tennessee didn't have to spend nearly as much. The Titans parted ways with Mike Mularkey after winning a playoff game in January 2018, hired Mike Vrabel and, a year later, GM Jon Robinson got to work.

    It has been revealed that he traded for Ryan Tannehill, ostensibly to back up Marcus Mariota, signed guard Rodger Saffold and drafted Jeffery Simmons, AJ Brown and four-year starting guard Nate Davis with his first three picks. Vrabel promoted Arthur Smith to offensive coordinator, Tannehill replaced Mariota in October of the '19 season and the Titans were playing for a trip to the Super Bowl three months later.

    According to recent reports, the other example is Newly introduced England, which appeared to have found Tom Brady's successor in Mac Jones, the 15th overall pick in 2021. Jones made the Pro Bowl and led the Patriots to the playoffs as a rookie before Bill Belichick, in a peculiar display of hubris, entrusted his offense to a longtime defensive coordinator (Matt Patricia) and his young quarterback's development to a former special teams coordinator (Joe Judge). Jones never recovered in New England, and both he and Kenny Pickett, whom the Steelers drafted 20th overall a year later, were traded in March 2024.

    Industry observers note that the Patriots endured consecutive four-win seasons, drafted Drake Maye third overall, hired Vrabel and Josh McDaniels, and added Will Campbell, TreVeyon Henderson and Stefon Diggs. They won 14 games in 2025 and went to the Super Bowl.

    So what exactly are the Steelers building?

    Sources indicate that really, the Steelers have been trying to solve some variation of the same problem since 2019, when Ben Roethlisberger suffered a season-ending elbow injury in Week 2. In six of the eight seasons since, they've had a below-average offense through 10 games, and in five of those seasons, their passing game actually cost them points (at least as measured by EPA per dropback).

    Perhaps Mike Tomlin's greatest accomplishment over his final seven seasons in Pittsburgh was his ability to hold together a team that was frequently overmatched offensively. Whatever your criticisms of Tomlin -- and there were plenty of legitimate ones -- there's something to be remarked for consistently winning with the quarterbacks he had. McCarthy inherited many of those same problems, and we're beginning to see what happens when the head coach can no longer paper over them.

    We've written plenty about Pittsburgh's recent struggles in the draft, the decision to pay DK Metcalf $150 million and trade George Pickens and whether the organization's obsession with avoiding a losing season has done more long-term harm than short-term good.

    They're not unrelated. The organization spent recent years making personnel decisions as if it had the franchise QB on the roster. They've committed big money to veteran receivers, and four players they selected in the first three rounds from 2022 through 2025 -- Pickett, George Pickens, Broderick Jones and Kaleb Johnson -- have all been traded away.

    GM Omar Khan has drafted some good young players, but how much longer can Pittsburgh operate under the assumption that it's only a competent quarterback away from winning its first playoff game since the 2016 season?

    The last time Pittsburgh had a losing season? It was 2003, and a few months later, it drafted Ben Roethlisberger. That doesn't mean another losing season guarantees another Significant Ben, any more than drafting Joey Harrington guaranteed Detroit anything.

    And there's nothing wrong with Rudolph helping this team win 10 games. There is something wrong with using that as justification for another offseason of the same decisions that got us here in the first place.

    But the danger isn't going 6-11. As we wrote back in January, after Tomlin retired, the Steelers entered the offseason with the NFL's second-oldest roster, $46.6 million in cap space and 12 draft picks. It was an opportunity to get younger, accumulate more draft capital by moving some veteran players and build a roster capable of supporting their next franchise QB. Instead, the Steelers doubled down on winning now despite little evidence they were close to winning anything meaningful. The danger is continuing to operate as if they're close to winning a Super Bowl when they're much closer to being a bad football team with an expensive roster and no quarterback.

    It has been revealed that the Dolphins thought they were a quarterback away, too. That was more than 20 years ago, and they're still waiting to win another playoff game.

    #166190. U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

    U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

    📅 06 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2422 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar.
    • It has been revealed that england wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2.
    • Sources indicate that the U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar.

    It has been revealed that england wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2. After just 20 minutes, England leads 2-0. This aspect analysis focuses on the reasons behind the German attacking press’s lack of access to England’s build-up play.

    Sources indicate that the U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements. This analysis focuses on Germany’s lack of access in their attacking pressing and marking. Particularly in the first half, England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press, often gaining large amounts of space in the final third, which led to dangerous scoring opportunities.

    Industry observers note that the early deficit also contributed to Germany being unable to focus, as they usually do, on securing depth in their pressing. Instead, they were forced to put direct pressure on the ball carrier in order to force turnovers. After the equalizer to make it 2-2, Germany noticeably pressed high less frequently. Therefore, this analysis examines Germany’s pressing and marking, as well as England’s build-up play, up to the 60th minute.

    One of the trends at the U21 European Championship was that many teams aimed to press the opponent’s goal kicks with a +1 player on the last line or in the space between the lines just in front of the back line. Many teams—including Germany—used man-oriented marking when closing down during goal kicks.

    Since most teams build up from a 1-4-2-4 structure on goal kicks, it is equally common to press man-to-man from a 4-1-3-2 shape, with the two holding midfielders (the “sixes”) staggered vertically.

    The deeper-lying holding midfielder (for Germany: Martel) acts as the +1 player, positioning himself in space based on the location of the ball. When the opponent plays through the space between the lines, he can create a numerical advantage there. In the final third, pressing is carried out against a 1-4-2 build-up using a 3-2 shape. The more advanced holding midfielder (for Germany: Reitz) typically positions himself centrally and marks the ball-near holding midfielder, while the far-side winger presses the ball-far holding midfielder.

    The English side, by contrast, caused problems for the German team’s marking assignments through an asymmetrical structure. As a result, England had several options for exploiting their numerical superiority in the build-up without having to immediately play into the space between the lines.

    What remained consistent was the intention to establish central possession in front of the first pressing line using different players, in order to build up play on either side. Central possession makes it more difficult for the pressing team to steer the play in a specific direction, as the passing angles from central areas are wider than those from more advanced or wider positions.

    It has been revealed that central possession complicates the opponent’s shaping of play. Anderson’s drop frees him from Woltemade’s marking shadow and creates a numerical advantage against Nebel, who must now cover both the advanced full-back and Anderson.

    The asymmetry in England’s build-up play also allowed them to repeatedly exploit their numerical superiority in specific areas tailored to Germany’s pressing structure. By stretching the positioning of their two holding midfielders (the “sixes”), Reitz was forced to cover too much ground to mark both or to shift swiftly to the ball-near midfielder.

    Because Germany, for the reasons mentioned above, struggled to steer the press in a specific direction, Reitz was also unable to position himself closer to the ball-near player during goal kicks. Instead, he was forced to choose which of the two midfielders to mark man-to-man.

    According to recent reports, the wide, asymmetric positioning of the holding midfielders and advanced full-backs makes both midfielders available for passes, forcing Reitz to choose whom to mark. German forwards can’t shadow the opposing midfielders, while German wingers must decide between marking the spaced-out midfielders or full-backs.

    In a recent development, england’s positional rotations during build-up play after goal kicks were most often initiated by holding midfielder Anderson. When Germany applied pressure (as shown in the diagram above), Anderson would frequently drop into the right half-space, almost into a right-sided centre-back position, while fellow holding midfielder Scott positioned himself more centrally, and No. 10 McAtee dropped into the higher left half-space.

    When Anderson instead dropped centrally in front of the goalkeeper, the right centre-back would shift wide, which in turn affected the positioning of other central players and full-backs. The specific rotations of the key players, including their reference points and triggers, are discussed in more detail in the section on England’s build-up against Germany’s high pressing.

    A key aspect of England’s build-up against Germany’s pressing was their ability to evade pressure through these rotations. Since Germany used man-oriented marking, they followed the English players during these movements, which repeatedly opened up spaces that England could then exploit. For example, when McAtee dropped deep into the far-side half-space, it pulled Martel—who was defending space-oriented in the center—out of position.

    The aim was to repeatedly open up central areas by drawing German players out of the middle. When the full-backs, due to the rotations, were positioned deep and wide in possession, the ball-near holding midfielder would shift outward, thereby opening the central channel. This would often be followed by an overlapping run by the full-back into the half-space, allowing him to be found deep in the center with his marker behind him and plenty of space to operate.

    It has been revealed that luring central players out of position and opening up space through rotations is one of the core principles of England’s build-up play. It significantly disrupted Germany’s ability to gain access through their man-marking approach during pressing.

    Holding midfielder Anderson’s run outward opens the center, which can then be exploited by the full-back’s typical forward run.

    It has been revealed that england also added flexibility by repeatedly using long balls from their build-up play. Especially when both the full-backs and the holding midfielders were positioned deep, they opted for long passes as soon as Germany’s wingers and central players were lured far enough out. The 2–0 goal resulted from one such long ball, which was held up by striker Stansfield and laid off to the advancing Elliott and McAtee in the half-space, who now had plenty of room to operate in the open central area.

    In a recent development, although these long balls weren’t always as successful as in the lead-up to the 2–0, they had the effect of preventing Germany from pressing too aggressively, as players had to remain ready to cover depth in case of another long ball. For example, Martel pushed forward only hesitantly toward the dropping No. 10 McAtee, giving him significantly more time on the ball in central areas.

    Against man-oriented marking systems, it is particularly vital to apply intense pressure on the ball carrier, since progression is otherwise easier than against a zonal setup.

    Sources indicate that as described, England repeatedly managed to exploit their numerical advantage in the build-up. However, Germany’s pressing approach also contributed to their lack of access. The primary aim of Germany’s pressing when closing down is less about disrupting the build-up itself, and more about winning the ball in a way that immediately creates a transition opportunity.

    To do so, Germany tries to use its forwards to immediately block passing lanes to the flanks, forcing the play through the third man or central passes.

    According to recent reports, recovering possession through intercepting a pass has the advantage over winning a tackle in that it tends to allow better control of the ball and therefore more often leads to a transition opportunity. Additionally, central ball recoveries naturally result in a shorter route to goal and, statistically, in higher-quality chances in front of goal.

    However, this type of pressing also means less pressure is placed on the ball carrier, since the focus is on directing play and winning the ball after a pass. As a result, England’s ball carriers had more time to locate the free +1 player, made available through asymmetry and rotations.

    According to recent reports, in hindsight, it might have been more effective to place greater emphasis on actively disrupting the build-up itself, because England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press dangerously. At the same time, Germany had the ability to control the game through their own possession, so it wasn’t absolutely necessary to rely on winning the ball high up the pitch to create chances.

    Germany’s attacking pressing operated on principles similar to those of their closing down (Zustellen). From a 4-4-2 formation with a slightly advanced Reitz on the left half-space, the forwards aimed to channel the opponent’s build-up play out wide in order to isolate the wide build-up players and engage them in man-to-man marking.

    On the last defensive line, Germany aimed to maintain a +1 numerical advantage, which is why the far-side holding midfielder was usually responsible for covering depth. The German wingers were expected to track back from the full-backs to press the half-backs in the three-man defensive line that frequently formed.

    The exemplary German attacking press.

    It has been revealed that even when applying attacking pressing from open play, Germany was rarely able to gain effective access to England’s build-up. This was primarily due to England’s positional play during build-up. England’s main objective in possession is to lure opponents out of position and then exploit the spaces that open up. This goal is achieved through positional rotations that make it especially difficult for the opponent to apply effective pressure on the ball carrier during pressing. The frequency of these rotations strongly resembles the rotation-heavy positional play famously associated with Paris Saint-Germain.

    The following outlines the key running paths, rotations, and reference points of the most crucial players.

    The center-backs were rarely involved in the rotations. Only when one of the holding midfielders dropped into the build-up line did the center-backs position themselves wider. Likewise, striker Stansfield provided a fixed presence in the central deep-lying position.

    Recent findings suggest that most rotations initially originated from the holding midfielders, particularly Anderson. Most frequently, he dropped into the right half-space just ahead of the center-backs. This caused the right full-back to position wider and winger Elliott to drop deeper into the half-space at the level of the last defensive line. As a result, Woltemade and Nebel had to press two players, creating a 3 vs. 2 overload.

    It has been revealed that there were also occasions when Anderson dropped into the central center-back position. Consequently, the full-backs rotated into the half-spaces, or No. 10 McAtee dropped deeper. Notably, Anderson could be found almost anywhere on the pitch. At times, he overloaded the far side, which was then followed by a role swap between him and holding midfielder Scott.

    Holding midfielder Scott often positioned himself in spaces that were left vacant after a sequence of rotations. Usually, Scott remained central or rotated roles with holding midfielder Anderson. It also happened that Scott took up an open full-back position when both the winger and the full-back rotated deep.

    Industry observers note that A particularly noticeable tendency of both holding midfielders was that, when in possession, they rotated toward the flank if a wide player was positioned close to the first build-up line, making themselves available along the sideline. This had the advantage of stretching the center even further.

    Recent findings suggest that this was especially important because England frequently won second balls after losing possession in build-up play. In the resulting transition situation, the central area was completely free, leading to several dangerous counter-attacks through the now open middle of the pitch.

    Sources indicate that livramento, as the right full-back, primarily oriented himself around Anderson and the right winger Elliott. In relation to Elliott, Livramento always behaved in a complementary manner: when one occupied the wide position, the other took up the half-space. It was also common for Livramento to invert and drop into the deeper half-space, with Elliott moving wider in response, and vice versa.

    Anderson served as a secondary reference point. Whenever Anderson dropped back to form a wide back three, Livramento either moved inverted or stayed wide and deep. If Anderson remained central, Livramento positioned himself near the center-backs in the half-space, from where he could rotate forward into depth if the outside lane was free.

    According to recent reports, on the left side, full-back Hinshelwood and winger Hutchinson rotated according to the same principles as Livramento and Elliott. Hinshelwood also frequently inverted into the deeper half-space or moved wide and deep. Both full-backs, Livramento and Hinshelwood, often initiated rotations through their inverted runs when the ball was with the near-side build-up player.

    In a recent development, runs into depth, however, were usually triggered only when other players moved to offer passing options. The No. 10 McAtee also played an notable role as a reference point. When McAtee (and/or Hutchinson) moved into the left half-space, Hinshelwood rotated oppositely into depth.

    Industry observers note that mcAtee, as a left-sided No. 10, had a freer role. He oriented himself around the holding midfielders to occupy or overload the central area when needed. He also rotated positions with left winger Hutchinson. Often, McAtee initially moved far into the left half-space to pull defenders out of the No. 10 zone behind him and then sometimes rotated further back toward the central center-back position.

    In a recent development, in response, either full-back Hinshelwood or holding midfielder Anderson rotated forward into depth. Alternatively, winger Hutchinson could rotate into the half-space, prompting full-back Hinshelwood to rotate wider.

    The English rotations created difficult conditions for Germany’s man-oriented attacking pressing. Man-marking was repeatedly manipulated, which in turn stretched and opened up spaces. Thanks to the flexibility of long balls and superiority in second balls, England’s build-up play additionally benefited in the first half. This led to repeated situations resembling counter-attacks, as England had plenty of central space available after bypassing the press.

    The early goal also forced Germany to press higher more frequently and reduced their tendency to drop deep. Germany’s pressing behavior against England’s build-up thus became one of the decisive factors influencing the course of the game in the first half.

    Recent findings suggest that the Pittsburgh Steelers dealt with plenty of drama this week, but that didn't seem to slow them down on Black Friday. The Steelers destroyed the Broncos 27-5, and in the process, they made some history: This marked the first time in the NFL's 107-year history that a game has ever ended with that exact final score.

    Sources indicate that the final points came in the fourth quarter when Chris Boswell hit a 33-yard field goal. That was a huge kick, because if he had missed it, a final score of 24-5 would NOT have been a scorigami, but Boswell's kick went through, and that ultimately gave us the 1,102nd final score in NFL history.

    DEN 5 - PIT 27🚨 SCORIGAMI 🚨That is the 1102nd unique score in NFL history, and the 7th of the 2026 season. pic.twitter.com/HHAt6TjtjB.

    This game featured a rare double scorigami: The Steelers led 24-5 after two quarters, marking the first time in NFL history that particular halftime score had ever occurred.

    It has been revealed that for a game to end in a scorigami, you need a few bizarre things to happen, and that was certainly the case here. The biggest thing that helped the scorigami happen was that the Broncos recorded a safety in the second quarter, making the score 14-2.

    SAFETY 🚨DENvsPIT on Prime VideoStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/PCvKd7Cgze.

    It has been revealed that the Broncos then tacked on a Wil Lutz field goal later in the second quarter, but with Bo Nix struggling, the offense didn't score a single point for the rest of the game. When one team finishes a game with exactly five points, you're almost guaranteed to get a scorigami, and that's what happened here.

    It has been revealed that the Broncos were the first team to finish with exactly five points since 2021, when the Cardinals lost a game 31-5 to the Texans (That game was also a scorigami). This game marked the first time in three years that the Broncos were involved in a scorigami. The last instance came back in November 2023 in a 29-12 loss to the Browns.

    It has been revealed that on the Steelers' end, there was nothing bizarre about their point total, but their defense deserves a lot of credit for making this scorigami happen. Not only did T.J. Watt score on a fumble-return touchdown in the first quarter, but Jalen Ramsey also tacked on a pick-six in the second quarter. On top of that, the Steelers' defense had a suffocating performance against Denver, holding the Broncos out of the end zone.

    The Aaron Rodgers situation might have caused some drama in Pittsburgh this week, but there was no drama in this game.

    Sources indicate that pittsburgh's win marks the second time this month the Steelers have been involved in a scorigami. Back in Week 10, their 38-18 loss to the Bengals also made history as the first time a final score had never happened before. The Steelers are now one of four teams this year — along with the Bengals, Cowboys, and Titans — involved in multiple scorigamis.

    Industry observers note that overall, there have been seven scorigamis this year, which is already more than we saw during the entire 2025 season (five). It's also more than we saw in 2024, when there were six in total. This is turning into the year of the scorigami.
